en: I first prostrate before Hari-Hara, who is adorned with a digit of the moon, whose face is auspicious, who is the treasure-house of Śiva, who is worshipped by the sages, and whose nature consists of the creation, preservation, and destruction [of the world]. (YRps 1.1)

I bow daily to Śāradā, who wears garments as white as a white water-lily or a jasmine flower, who is beautifully adorned with necklaces of pure pearls, and who is served even by all the hosts of Siddhas.
I first bow down to Gaṇapati, whose elephantine face has the luster of a broken cloud, who possesses three eyes and four short arms, and whose crest is beautifully adorned with gold and jewels.
The abode of Giriśa is eternally great and wondrous, the supreme destroyer of all diseases,
proficient in the entire collection of supernatural powers, the remover of the sins of those who bow before it, and the one who leads beyond the cycle of existence.
(Contents) First, I shall describe the origin of mercury exactly as it is;
thereafter, its purification and likewise its eighteen operations.
The fourfold knowledge of binding, the reduction of mercury to ashes,
the purification of the metals, their killing, and the description of their qualities.
Indeed, I shall here properly describe the eight great minerals (mahārasas),
as well as the qualities, purification, and killing of the secondary minerals (uparasas).
And I shall explain in detail for all of them the melting and casting [of metals],
as well as the virtues and defects of gems, along with their purification and killing.

I shall describe in detail the processes of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), coloring (*rañjana*), liquefaction (*druti*), and amalgamation (*melānaka*) regarding mercury, as well as the hundreds of varieties of mercury itself.
The divisions of medicinal herbs are declared to be exactly four:
divine herbs, herbal juices, perfected herbs, and others.
Thus have been briefly described the great medicinal herbs, as well as the yantras, the puṭas, the crucibles for metals, and the various curiosities.
And aphrodisiac formulations that increase semen and sexual vigor have been included in this treatise, neither too concisely nor too elaborately. (YRps 1.12)
(Yoginī-hṛdaya: Origin of the Sūta) To the west of the Himalayas, there is a beautiful mountain named Girīndra;
in its vicinity, within an exceedingly well-formed well, this very Lord of Mercury (Rasendra) dwells in person. (YRps 1.13)
Endowed with the beauty and qualities of a young maiden, well-adorned and mounted upon an excellent horse, she arrived there looking down at the well; then, she turned back with great speed.
The excellent charioteer, having run about in the four directions, has surely fallen to the ground.
The field extending twelve yojanas all around the mountain is said to be perfectly circular, vast, and well-proportioned for the one who has brought forth [the seed].
When that clay is cast into the crucible, it indeed becomes the destroyer of disease;
it arises as something truly beautiful and is called mercury itself.
Regarding the subtypes of mercury by caste (following its emergence from the well):
"The mercury, having emerged from the well, becomes a twice-born [caste] as it proceeds in the four directions."
Indeed, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra are born from the four [classes].
The complexion [of Mercury] arises as white, black, yellow, and red,
respectively in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions. (YRps 1.19)
White mercury is used in white rites, and black mercury likewise serves as the producer of the body.
The yellow-colored [stone] is a maker of gold; the red one is a destroyer of disease.
When all [these] are unified, they always accomplish every task;
when practiced, they destroy all diseases and bestow all supernatural attainments (*siddhi*).
Thus, having understood that which arises from the Sūta, one is indeed not afflicted by diseases;
for it has been purified, killed, transmuted, and refined, becoming auspicious.
(The eight purificatory processes or operations of mercury): Sweating, rubbing, and indeed fainting which arises therefrom;
falling, blocking, proper restraining, and inflaming. (YRps 1.23)
Likewise, there is the gradual process of ingesting and circulating the "bite" (grāsa) of mica;
indeed, internal liquefaction (garbhadruti), external liquefaction (bāhyadruti), and digestion (jāraṇa) have been thus described.
Sāraṇa, krāmaṇa, vedha, rañjana, and sevana—these indeed are the eighteen operations of mercury;
their names have been stated by me here in brief. (YRps 1.25)
(The defects of mercury: Five defects have been declared for mercurial preparations by the best of physicians:
dross, poison, fire, intoxication, and pride, respectively.
They cause fainting, death, intoxication, pustules, and dizziness of the head.
(Regarding the mercury-coatings:
I shall describe the seven coatings of mercury according to their true nature;
I shall state their names in accordance with the *Devīśāstra*. (YRps 1.27)
Arising from clay, stone, water, metal, iron, lead, and tin—
these are the seven sheaths in the embryo, and they are indeed like poison.
Indeed, there are exactly twelve defects by which mercury is expelled by the twice-born;
for them, there is no accomplishment of the essence (*rasasiddhi*), while others are like Yama himself.
Therefore, the removal of defects must be performed by the most excellent physicians.
There, one should perform the sweating [process] at the proper time on an auspicious day;
the sweating of mercury should be carried out by practitioners using a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus). (YRps 1.30)
The two alkalis combined with sour [substances], as well as the five pungents, the three aromatics (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), and citraka; YRps 1.31.
One should grind together all the medicinal herbs— puṣpaka, kāsīsa, and saurāṣṭrī—
in equal parts with one-eighth part of mercury.
Having prepared a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should place mercury in its center and wrap it with a fine cloth or a birch-bark leaf three times over.
Indeed, one should tie a small pouch of mercury to a piece of wood by means of a cord and suspend it from a vessel filled with water infused with husks.
One should properly apply fomentation for three days; that is declared to be fomentation.
(2. Mardana) Now, I shall describe in detail and exactly as it is the process of *mardana*, by which the most pure mercury is produced. (YRps 1.36)
One should indeed grind the mercury in a mortar for three days;
now, therefore, I shall describe the dimensions of that mortar.
Its length shall be one kalā and nine aṅgulas, and its height likewise nine aṅgulas;
one should make it six aṅgulas in width and depth.
The width at the back is two finger-breadths, and it is made very smooth in the middle;
the pestle here is ten finger-breadths long and shaped like a half-moon.
(Continuation of *mardana*):
One should grind the king of mercury (*rasarāja*) with five *palas* of *sūta* [iron] in *kāñjika* for three days; this certainly serves to destroy external impurities. (YRps 1.40)
Immediately thereafter, one should wash it with warm *kāñjika* water.
(3. Mūrchana) Hereafter, I shall explain the mūrchana of mercury;
this mūrchana is free from defects and destroys the seven coatings.
One should grind together svarjikā, yavaśūka, as well as the five pungents (paṭupañcaka), all sour medicinal substances, and mercury.
It should remain in the mortar for three days until it reaches a state of dissolution;
this process, occurring through the destruction of its original form, is here called *mūrcchana*.
It then attains purity, and the breaking of the knots occurs.

(4. Utthāpana) Now, the rite of "raising up" (*utthāpana*) for mercury must be performed with great effort by the best of physicians according to the path of the science of alchemy (*rasaśāstra*). YRps 1.45.
Then it should be subjected to sudation in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) for three days as previously described;
thereafter, it should be rubbed on a stone slab in the sun's heat for one day. This constitutes the proper "arousing" (*utthāpana*), which destroys the defect of fainting (*mūrchā*).
(5. *Pātana*) Indeed, I shall explain in great detail the great practice of *pātana*, which is said to be threefold and serves to destroy the defects of mercury (*rasa*). (YRps 1.47)
Indeed, there are upward sublimation, downward precipitation, and lateral transmutation in sequence.
Herein is described the characteristic of the upward sublimation apparatus (*ūrdhvapātanayantra*).
A clay vessel should be made, elevated by six finger-breadths.
A second auspicious vessel should be made with this measurement: seven finger-breadths in length at the mouth and thirty finger-breadths in circumference.
One should grind mercury with the two alkalis, asafoetida, and likewise the five salts, combined with the group of sour substances (amlavarga).
One should smear that paste upon the auspicious lower vessel,
place the upper vessel facing downwards over it, and thus perform the sealing (*saṃpuṭa*).
One should prepare a seal there using ash and salt;
then, having placed a pot on the stove, one should kindle a fire of grain there.
Above that, a water vessel should be placed for a period of four watches;
once its own temperature has become cool, one should cause the fluid to ascend.
Thus, this is proclaimed as the *ūrdhvapātanayantra* (upward-descending apparatus).
(5.2. *adhaḥpātana*) One should properly invert the aforementioned crucible into a muddy [vessel].
Once she has been placed in the pit, one should kindle a fire upon her head.
When the mercury falls downward for a period of three watches (yāmas),
this is indeed proclaimed by those who know the alchemical art as the *adhaḥpātana* (downward-falling) apparatus.
(5.3. Tiryakpātana) One should grind the king of mercury together with the aforementioned medicinal herbs;
having poured the mercury into a horizontal jar, another jar should indeed be placed upon its mouth.
The younger [brother] should have a hole made in his belly, and within that hole, the best of physicians should cause an iron tube to be inserted; this tube should be connected to a water vessel.
The wise one should ignite a fierce fire beneath the mercury apparatus for a period of three watches (yāmas), until the mercury undergoes lateral distillation.
Indeed, the triad of yantras and pātanās is easy to perform.
For this has been correctly explained by me through the illustration of the arrival of the vital essence (rasa).
(6. Rodhana) Now I shall describe the practice of restraining the *rasa*,
by means of which the state of being a mere "pala" of the king of *rasas* is indeed pacified.
One should place ten palas of Sindhu-salt and three prasthas of water inside a jar, along with mercury that is free from defects.
Just as [a vessel] is properly sealed with clay by means of a cover,
one should indeed hold it for three days in a windless and secluded place.
O King of Physicians, perform the restraint in this very manner.
(7. Niyāmana) Hereafter, I shall explain the fixation (*niyāmana*) of mercury (*pārada*). Indeed, the best of essences, combined with water and rock salt, should be placed within a jar.
And having been sweated for three days, even one who is vigorous becomes [so] again.
(8. Illumination) Now, therefore, I shall explain the illumination of the king of essences (*rasarāja*), by means of which hunger and pervasiveness are produced. YRps 1.66.
Mustard seeds combined with salt, black pepper, drumstick (*śigru*), and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*),
together with green vitriol (*kāsīsa*) and potassium carbonate (*kāṅkṣī*), mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
Having soaked it for three days, one should then rub it with alkali;
by this very method, the process of ignition (*dīpana*) certainly occurs.
Intensity, the quality of producing momentum, pervasiveness, hunger,
and especially strength arise perfectly once [the practice] has been performed.
(8.1. Illumination:
Producing the Opening) Indeed, the method for illumination is the action that produces the opening;
I shall describe, in brief and according to the facts, the purification of the *rasas*.
Then, the mercury should be rubbed with gold weighing one-eighteenth part [of the mercury] and with lime juice for one day thereafter.
Indeed, having been fomented with alkaline substances, salts, and pleasant [herbs], and then washed with *kāñjika* itself, the mouth becomes fit for eating. (YRps 1.72)

(8.2. Illumination: Producing the Mouth [2]) One should grind the essence of the metal (tāpyasattva) with a sixteenth part of gold and twice that amount of heated iron filings while it is hot. YRps 1.73.
Indeed, having made it manifest with the juice of *rasacukra* and the alkali of chickpeas,
one should rub it twenty-one times with the waters of *jaṃbīra* and *pūraka*.
One should indeed rub each [ingredient] for one watch (yāma) during the day;
thus the mouth of the *yātudhāna* is properly [cleansed], there is no doubt.
Thus, this second method of kindling has been described by me;
furthermore, the eight purificatory rites for mercury have been explained in relation to the work upon the body.
And likewise, there are indeed ten practices that produce a body of steel.
(9. *Grāsamāna*) Now, I shall explain the consumption of mica (*abhra*).
A metal crucible must be properly prepared according to the *karoṭi* method.
By means of the application of a water-wheel, mercury, when combined with feces, certainly devours mouthfuls of mica; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the characteristics of the water-machine (*jalayantra*) are described by me:
a well-rounded iron vessel containing three *āḍhaka* measures of water.
In the middle of that, one should properly prepare a very firm iron casket;
inside this iron casket, pure mercury is to be placed.
One should carefully add sixteen parts of *viḍa* salt and sixty-four parts of mineral essence (*abhra-sattva*) into the crucible.
Thereafter, one should seal the casket with firm clay mixed with water,
or even with fire-clay, and ensure that the joints are completely closed.
Having placed that machine upon the hearth and filled it with warm water,
one should indeed apply fire gradually for exactly half a day.
When this has been done, one should consume the measure of the morsel; there is no doubt in this matter.
By this very method, one should certainly consume six morsels.
When the essence of the cloud (mercury) has been consumed, it bestows success in all undertakings;
for who, being devoid of pride, would not be able to perform that which is called "the crushing of pride"? (YRps 1.86)
Therefore, I shall describe the process of purification as it has been taught:
by taking sixty-four parts of mercury, one produces the "mouth" [of the mercury] using seed-substances (*bīja*).
Thereafter, the supreme seed should be given as one thirty-second part;
then, one should place a morsel of the seed as one sixteenth part.
The best of physicians should administer [the medicine] with one-eighth part of the liquid;
thus, the dose is given with a fourth part.
And likewise, one should accomplish it with an equal portion and by means of the *grāsa* alone;
when combined with a sixteenth part of *biḍa*, the mercury becomes hungry.
When the swallowed morsel has become digested and has indeed been passed as feces, [then one should proceed].
Viḍa salt, kāsīsa, rock salt, sauvarcala, and surāṣṭra,
combined with an equal amount of sulphur— this is *viḍa*, which acts as a digestive fire-stimulant.
(10. Cāraṇa) Now I shall describe, exactly as it is, the process of *cāraṇa* for the liquefied essence (*garbhadruti*), which increases its qualities and grants success to the King of Rasas.
Equal parts of iron filings, mica, and copper drawn out by sound should all be smelted together with a fire of khadira wood.
Using two bellows, one should cause that essence of mica— until only the mica remains—
to be ingested by the mercury in equal proportions.
In this very manner, the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of mercury should be performed three times; indeed, this is called the internal digestion (*garbhadruti-jāraṇa*) by the best of physicians. (YRps 1.96)

(12. External Alchemy) Now the procedure for external alchemy is indeed told according to the path of the Guru: "The essence of mica [is placed] in a crucible with the juice of *vajravallī*. (YRps 1.97)
When blown with *sauvarcala* salt, it takes on the form of mercury; this occurs when an equal amount of mercury has been mixed with the liquefied mica (*abhradruti*).
By that, it attains the state of being bound; thus, that external liquefaction is described.
Indeed, the practice of the rite of external liquefaction is accomplished through devotion to Śiva.
Through the grace of the Guru, by the constant worship of Mahābhairava,
and indeed by the worship of Śiva and Śivā, the external melting (druti) is accomplished.
(13. Jāraṇa) Now I shall describe in great detail the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
Having made equal parts of mica (*abhraka*) and the essence of iron pyrite (*tāpyasattva*), one should thoroughly heat them together.
Whatever essence remains after being reduced to ash, one should digest that essence within the mercury;
in this very manner, one should indeed accomplish the essence of mica by means of the two types of putrid substances.
Through the practice of alchemy, one becomes a maker of metals, but not a maker of the body;
for the two great and terrible powers of the elephant and the penis are indeed to be avoided at all times.
That perfected, dense essence, resembling semen yet like menstrual blood,
was placed in the mouth of one craving the flavor, in a quantity of only a single *valla*.
Even a fourth part of a *gadyāṇaka* is said to be the proper dose;
indeed, sour [juice] placed in a copper vessel, combined with *saindhava* salt.
Or even when combined with milk and processed for two days,
the resulting blue paste, which is equal in quality to *tuttha*, is so described by the wise.
One should grind the mercury together with this paste for three days in a heated mortar, and afterwards wash it with *kāñjika* vinegar.
One should place it in a bell-metal vessel; then, one should place the vitriol (viḍa) above and below that.
Thereafter, one should form a casket using one-eighth part of the mercury.
Having blocked the mouth with birch bark, one should wrap it with thread;
then, having wrapped the sealed vessel with a cloth, one should heat it in a swinging oven (*dolā*).
Every day, [the practitioner should perform the practice] in a vessel of stone, iron, or glass, using cow urine, the group of acidic substances, or sour gruel (kāñjika).
Then, having washed the juice with warm *kāñjika* water,
one should place it in a strong cloth four times its size and extract the juice by pressing from below.
But if even all the mercury falls into another vessel,
then the mercury, having properly digested the mica, becomes a wielder of the staff.
Furthermore, while digesting [the mercury], the unsurpassed seed of the clouds (abhrabīja) should be given;
indeed, by means of eight morsels, one should cause everything to be assimilated according to the path of the Guru.
When this is done, the mercury becomes equalized and certainly dissolves during the *sūtaka* stage;
however, I have not heard of such a perfect digestion (*jāraṇa*) being achieved by one's own hand.
When mercury has been properly processed with an equal amount of mica through *jāraṇa*, it becomes a "wielder of the staff" (*daṇḍadhārī*);
it is also called "infant" (*bāla*), and it will perform some small task. (YRps 1.115)

When the mica (abhraka) has been digested twice or thrice its weight, it is indeed described by me here as "youthful" (kiśora); when it has been digested four times its weight, it is described by me as "adolescent" (kiśora).
When the *abhraka* has been processed five times, the excellent mercury becomes young;
when the *abhraka* has been processed six times, the excellent mercury becomes old.
When mercury has been processed with iron seven or eight times and has become fully matured, it is called *ativṛddhaka*;
this very mercury brings about all accomplishments; it is mercury itself.
In this very manner, one should digest all metals.
(14. Sāraṇa) Now,
I shall explain the cause for the increase of piercing (*vedha*),
which is the *sāraṇa* that brings about great accomplishment for all ritual actions.
The crucible, resembling the *dhūrta* flower in shape, should be eight fingers long,
very wide at the mouth, and measured at four fingers [in width].
That [crucible] is also made of clay, dried, and highly polished in the middle;
the other [lid] is a cover for the crucible, very deep and provided with holes.
One should place pure, well-digested mercury (*sūta*) inside a crucible (*mūṣā*). [The ingredients for] the *sāraṇā* oil are fish,
turtles, frogs, leeches, rams, and pigs.
Having combined these together, one should likewise prepare a binding oil (*sāraṇa-taila*) consisting of *bhūnāga* excrement,
honey, and the feces of crows.
In the same way, one should prescribe a paste (kalka) of locusts and the like, as well as the impurity from the ears of a buffalo,
using a sixteenth part of the mercury.
Having filtered it with a cloth, one should place it into oil;
(this is *sāraṇā* [continued]). For the purpose of *sāraṇā*, one should thoroughly cook it in that oil.
Having mixed the seed with a paste, one should place it upon the crucible;
one should then seal the mouth of the crucible with a second lid.
One should seal the pair of crucibles with ash and salt;
having dug a hole one-third the size of the crucible, one should bury it in the earth.
Thereafter, one should properly blow it with a fierce fire using firm charcoal;
thus thoroughly incinerated, the seed falls abundantly into the midst of the mercury.
The lord of mercury, when processed with a flux, becomes endowed with qualities;
having first been liquefied and then processed, it bestows all accomplishments.
How could that which has not been refined and integrated become a cause of bondage?
Through the instruction of the Guru, the practice of integration is seen to be the supreme action.
That which has been properly heard is not truly realized through the mere application of manual experience.

Krāmaṇa) Now, the process of transference (*krāmaṇa*) for mercury is being described according to the scriptures; indeed, when performed correctly, it causes the mercury to transfer [its qualities]. (YRps 1.133)
One should take the earwax of the queens, women’s milk, and borax;
having made these substances equal in quantity, one should grind them together for a day.
Poison, cinnabar, mercury, red-antimony,
and *indragopa*, as well as *tuvarī*, honey, and crow-dung.
One should place this paste above and below, with the mercury (sūta) in the middle;
then, having added glass powder, one should heat it in a sealed crucible (andhamūṣā).
By this very transmutative process, mercury transmutes in an instant;
this is the most excellent transmutative agent, as spoken by Nandirāja.
Likewise, it penetrates without doubt the essence of mica, as well as lead, pure mercury,
and the seeds of mercury.
(16. Piercing) Now, I shall explain in great detail the procedure for piercing, by the mere knowledge of which a person becomes a knower of piercing. YRps 1.139.
Oil from the dhūrta plant, oil from the snake's phlegm, oil from the kaṅguṇī plant, oil from the bhṛṅgī plant, poison, and oil produced from nutmeg; YRps_1.140 //
Know that *hayamāraśiphātaila*, *abdheḥśoṣakatailaka*,
and these other oils are also *vedhakara* (penetrating).
When rubbed together with the perfected mercury (siddhasūta), it becomes a penetrator (vedhakṛt).
(The varieties of piercing: Piercing by smearing, as well as throwing, and likewise piercing with a spear.
The piercing by sound is called "smoke"; thus it is remembered as being fivefold.
[Regarding] the piercing by application (*lepavedha*): thin copper leaves and those made of silver (*kaladhūta*),
One should heat those very [substances] smeared with a paste using an *andhamūṣā* crucible.
When it has become cool, one should remove it; then the application and piercing (*lepa-vedha*) are described.
Alternatively, when the copper or silver is molten, one should pour the mercury (*rasa*) into it. (This is *kṣepa-vedha*.)
By means of that, one pierces suddenly; this is called *kṣepavedha* (the piercing by casting).
It melts silver, lead, copper, and likewise inferior metals. (This is *kuntavedha*).
When mercury has been melted in one or another vessel and [the powder] is applied to it,
those who know the scriptures say that there occurs "piercing with a needle" (kuntavedha).
Through the touch of smoke, the metals gold and silver are produced;
that is certainly to be known as *dhūmavedha* (smoke-penetration) of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*).
When the supreme mercury is bound, a sound is produced directly from its touch;
in that very same way, a piercing occurs, and that is called "piercing by sound" (śabdavedha).
(17. Rañjana) Now, therefore, I shall explain the coloring (*rañjana*) of mercury (*pārada*);
for when it is colored and transmuted, it is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) himself in manifest form.
Coloring is performed with iron, copper, and mercury;
likewise, it should be carried out with the red group [of minerals] according to the path of the scriptures.
Then, the coloring of mercury should be performed with the dye of *gandharāja*,
as well as with copper, red glass, and red rock salt.
One should color the mercury contained within a blind crucible using copper and other metals;
one should color it with the pigment of sulphur (gandha) by means of the application of the *iṣṭikā* vessel.
And by means of the color of mercury and through the application of a balance-scale,
one should always dye the quicksilver by rubbing it with the powder of *tīkṣṇa* (steel).
By means of copper reduced to a paste, one should keep [the mercury] for seven days;
the coloring of the king of alchemical elixirs occurs— of this there is no doubt.
A crucible made of clay should be prepared and smeared with the red group of substances;
having placed mercury in its center, by means of heating, it becomes colored. (YRps 1.156)
I have indeed briefly described the coloring of mercury;
for according to the path of the scriptures, many methods of coloring have been demonstrated.
(18. Sevana) Now, the practice of *sevana*, which consists of eighteen parts of mercury, is here being described by me with effort and in detail. YRps 1.158.
When attended with effort according to the path of the scriptures, the *sūta* bestows perfection;
otherwise, even if swallowed, it would kill a person like poison.
First, having performed emesis, one should subsequently carry out purgation;
then one should consume dead mercury (mṛtābhra), and afterwards the service of mercury (sūta).
The excellent, pure, and well-refined mercury, which always acts upon the body and metals,
becomes the destroyer of all diseases and the bestower of all accomplishments when practiced.
To whatever extent a gadyāṇa of iron becomes a penetrator [of mercury],
to that same extent, when consumed, it destroys the diseases of the body.
Then, the juice should be the size of a *valla*—that is, a *rājikā*, a *priyaṅgu*, a *sarṣapa*, a *mudga*, a *māṣaka*, a *raktikā*, or a *caṇaka*. (YRps 1.163)
This is the dosage for the elixir proclaimed by those skilled in all practices;
one should consume it with a post-digestive drink (anupāna) along with a piece of betel leaf.
When the *sūtra* has been practiced in this manner, one is liberated from all diseases;
freed from all sins, one attains the supreme goal.
YRps, Chapter 2 (Pāradabandha):
Now, therefore, I shall explain the fixation of the king of mercury.
Indeed, something has been experienced by me through the grace of my gurus.
Bondage is said to be of four types: *jalaukā*, *khoṭa*, *pāṭaka*, and [the fourth].
Likewise, that which is called "ashes" (bhasman) has been explicitly taught in the Rasāgama.
The "cooked bond" (pakvabandha) is like a leech; the "pill-bond" (piṣṭīstambha), however, is a *khoṭaka*.
The "flattened bond" (*pāṭa*) is a *parpaṭikā*; the "ash-bond" (*bhasmabandha*) becomes like ashes. (YRps 2.3)
In this context, the root-substance, the gem, gold, lead,
and tin— these four are the causes for the binding of mercury.
The binding by roots (mūlikābandha) is the best; the binding by the wrist (maṇibandha) is middling;
the binding by minerals (dhātubandha) is inferior; and the binding by puti-herbs (pūtibandha) is the lowest of the low.
This fifth [type] is the *drutibandha*, which always effects the transformation of the body and metals;
it is to be recognized by the best of physicians through the specific liquefaction (*druti*) of mica (*abhra*).
I shall now describe this binding of the root-herbs (*mūlikābandha*), which follows in sequence, regarding mercury:
purified mercury, as well as mercury that has been processed with *rākṣasavaktra* and *abhraka*.
Mercury, rubbed for three days in the resinous exudate from the root of the *iṅgudī* tree,
should then be removed and bound in a cloth by the physician.
One should perform steaming in fermented rice-water (kāñjika) for a fixed period of seven days;
once cooked, it should be kept within cooked food for the duration of a year.
Then, having placed it upon the fruit of the *dhūrta* plant, one should sweat it a hundred times;
this [substance] is cooked in great oil, in *dhūrta* oil, and in a mass of food.
When bound by that method, hardness is produced;
it certainly brings about the complete immobilization of mercury, without a doubt. (YRps 2.11)
Held directly in the mouth, this always causes the paralysis of semen;
indeed, this is declared to be the sole method for binding mercury with a root-plant.
(Second Root-Binding) Now, there is another method for the binding of mercury as well:
one should rub it with the juices of the roots of *nāgārjuni* for seven days. (YRps 2.12)
Then, ground with neem wood that has been chewed in the mouth,
the mercury becomes as smooth as fresh butter.
Having bound it with a cloth, one should place the fruit inside a hollowed-out gourd;
wrapped in cow dung, one should cook it over a fire of dried cow-dung.
One should properly roast [the medicine] a hundred times in a crucible called *lāvaka*, increasing the number of roastings gradually;
for a period of three months, one should cook it in the midst of food.
Afterwards, one should give a hundred layers of dried cow-dung cakes as before;
by this very method, the mercury (sūtaka) is always bound.
This yoga of direct perception has indeed been taught for the practitioner.
When properly held in the mouth, it is supremely effective in paralyzing semen;
likewise, it paralyzes mercury, and when bound, it is fully capable of paralyzing tin as well. (YRps 2.17)
(Mūlikābandha) One should diligently grind purified mercury with well-digested mica for one day using the juice of the root of the *arka* plant.
Then, a very firm and polished crucible made of *vajra* should be prepared and smeared with a paste made from the root of the *arka* plant.
Having placed the mercury in the middle of a crucible, one should seal it with another crucible;
when heated properly for half a watch (three hours), the mercury-khoṭa is produced.
Having recognized that the mercury-cake has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract it;
held in the mouth for just one year, it destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
This [mercury], when bound by means of medicinal roots, brings about all accomplishments;
indeed, the binding by means of medicinal roots was truly performed by Nāgārjuna and others.
It is the most excellent, effecting all accomplishments and always performing every task.
(4) Having properly purified the excellent mercury and likewise caused it to be swallowed by the *ambara*,
one should subsequently grind it with the juices of the *jalakūmbhī* for seven days.
One should fashion a crucible for it and place the mercury (sūtaka) therein;
one should then seal the mercury-crucible within another blind crucible.
In that case, a packet should be given by one forest-dweller;
in this manner, packets should be given, increasing by one lotus each time.
In this very manner, one should cause three layers (puṭas) to be applied;
thus the lord of mercury attains fixation, just as the word of the Guru is true.

Having carefully and constantly reduced the seeds of *dhūrta* to powder, one should cause them to fall through the upward-acting apparatus (*ūrdhvayantra*), making them equal to the king of mercury (*sūtarāja*). (Mūlikābandha 5) YRps 2.28.
Then, one should indeed place it in a mortar twenty-one times and grind it for seven days in the resin of *iṅgudī* leaves.
Having thoroughly ground [the ingredients] with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, with the ash of burnt poison (*viṣakharparaka*), with the juice of *pāṭhā*, and indeed with the fresh juice of *lajjālū*.
Having massaged it every three days, it certainly attains firmness;
having been thoroughly steamed with the swinging-iron apparatus (*dolāyantra*) for seven days in mercury produced from *dhūrta* (datura).
Having placed it inside a crucible made of lead and within the flesh of a pig, one should fry it with *dhūrta* oil; after seven days, the face [of the practitioner] is produced.
It becomes hard like a diamond; there is no doubt about this.
It constantly dries up the milk for the sake of the ritual marvel; of this there is no doubt.
Vīrya (mercury) certainly solidifies vaṅga (tin); this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Five methods have been described for the binding of the king of minerals (mercury).
(1) By Vajrasattva, the binding of mercury is achieved through a hundred piercings.
Having examined the various treatises on mercury, I shall now explain the second method, the Vajrabandha, in its proper sequence and exactly as it is. (YRps 2.35)
The wise one should cause vajrasattva and likewise sūta to be made in equal parts;
he should grind these three together with gold equal to one-quarter of the mercury.
Then one should indeed saturate it with the juice of the root of *vaṃdhyākarkoṭikā*, as well as with the juice of *dhūrta* and the juice of *citraka*. (YRps 2.37)
One should likewise strain the juice of these regulating [plants] through a cloth, using either *kāmbojī* juice or the juice of *nāḍī*.
One should rub the ball, placed inside a blind crucible (andhamūṣā), for one day at a time in this sequence under the heat of the sun, and then seal it with a firm seal.
Then, having been placed inside a metal casket and firmly sealed,
it was indeed blown with a bellows for a duration of two ghaṭikās.
Having ascertained that it has become cool to the touch of one's own body, they should take the mouse;
then, having carefully dug it up again and again, one should collect the mercury ash (sūtabhasma).
When that globule is heated with the addition of glass and borax, the mercury penetrates it by means of a hundredfold penetration; of this there is no doubt.
Situated in the mouth, it destroys death; it becomes the maker of the body and of iron.
(7) The Binding of Mercury by means of Vajra-Ashes: Having made equal parts of vajra-ashes and mercury, one should grind them together with the juice of *trinemikā*, *vajravallī*, and *sahadevī*.
For seven days, one should dry a perfectly round ball of mercury in the intense heat of the sun using the milky sap of the *snuhī* plant; then, once it is dried, one should apply a coating over it.
One should indeed apply a plaster seven times with the juice of *kākamācī*, with the fresh juice of *lāṅgalī*, and with the juice of *gojihvikā*.
One should seal the globule contained within a diamond crucible with a firm seal;
it is placed in the middle, enclosed within a crucible made of an iron casket.
Properly plaster it with seven layers of clay and rags, making it very firm; heat it strongly with charcoal embers and then allow it to cool while remaining in that state.
Having pierced the mercury contained in the crucible so that it becomes a solid mass (khoṭa) resembling a star,
bright and capable of performing all tasks, it becomes colored and a performer of transmutation (vedha).

(8) Binding the Mercury by means of the liquefaction of mica: One should grind the mercury together with the liquefied mica on a slab of stone for three watches (*yāma*) without interruption, using an equal amount [of the mica].
Combined with musk and camphor, along with black agallochum, sugar,
garlic, and asafoetida.
Likewise, mercury (sūtaka) should be rubbed with the juice of palāśa flowers and with fluxes (drutis) by means of the sun's heat.
They will certainly meet, there is no doubt; what is the use of further prolixity?
Therefore, by means of the juice of *guñjā* and white *vṛścīvaka*, [the desired result follows].
And with the juices of the lāṅgalī plant, [one should proceed] until the binding occurs.
Then, one should blow for a moment with five pieces of charcoal upon the illuminated crucible;
it attains a firm bond with speed, just as a lotus does at sunrise.
Indeed, when combined with the flux of mica, the lord of mercury is truly bound;
he becomes a direct devotee of Śiva, truthful in speech, and one whose senses are restrained.
The perfect union of the two Śivas will take place in his hand;
it is that which has been proclaimed in the Rasāgamas as the binding of mercury.
That has been clearly explained by me, yet it has neither been experienced nor practiced.
(9) The Binding of Mercury through Vajra-Melting:
The melting of *vajras* of the *brahma* species, measuring one *vallā*, and one *tolaka* of pure mercury should be ground together with the juice of the *kanyā* plant. (YRps 2.59)
One should grind that thoroughly until it becomes a fine paste,
having prepared a clean, level crucible made of burnt stone.
Having placed the dough-mass in the middle of that, one should make a lid for the poison of the snake equal in measure to the dough,
and then block the opening with it.
One should place the auspicious mouse in the middle of a bell-metal vessel,
and four vessels should be positioned in the four directions.
It is wonderful that mercury enters into bondage through its connection with heat;
this has been stated very clearly by Śiva as occurring daily during the intense heat of the sun.
Through union with the adamantine fluidity, the mercury attains a state of binding;
this is declared to be the truth, the most excellent among all methods of binding mercury.
(10) [The Binding of Mercury by the Flowing Gold]:
Now, I shall explain the binding of the king of elixirs (sūtarāja).
One should grind flowing gold with the lord of elixirs (rasendra) for seven days.
Washed with the juice of *Jvālāmukhī* and subsequently with *kāñjika*, one should wash [the instrument] every day; indeed, at night with the aforementioned juice and during the day with the other.
Subsequently, having placed it in a blind crucible, one should coat it seven times with a mixture of clay and rags; then, one should bury the ball in a pit in the ground.
Twelve finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in depth—
this is clearly stated by the lineage of the Guru to be the measurement for the excavation.
There, a lid should be placed on top with elephant dung and dried cow-dung;
in exactly twelve watches (yāmas), the mercury itself becomes bound.
When mercury is bound within the liquefaction of gold, it perfects the body and metals;
it is glorious, bestowing all accomplishments, and destroying old age and poverty.
(The binding of mercury by means of gold): This third [method], the binding of the metal, has been performed by my own hand;
therefore, I shall explain it exactly as it is for the sake of the practitioner. (YRps 2.71)
One should have thin leaves made of gold, like those of the *bhūrja* tree;
these should be the size of a *kola*, and the mercury (*sūtaka*) should weigh one *pala*.
One should grind it incessantly for one day with the juice of *nimbuka* fruits;
then, having formed that into a ball, one should place it upon a shallow earthen dish (*kharpara*).
It should be placed on the hearth and sprinkled with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla);
the dough must be kept firm for a fixed period of three days. (YRps 2.74)
Then, one should cause it to sweat for seven days using *dhūrtarasa* alone,
along with white *punarnavā*, *ciñcā*, *sahadevī*, and *nīlikā*.
Likewise, the *dhūrtavadhū*, the *lāṅgalī*, the *suradālikā*,
and the *sūtabandhakara* are declared by Nāgārjuna and others to be the most excellent.
One should smear the mercury-ball with the juices and pastes of these [plants];
thereafter, one should wrap it with triple layers of birch bark.
Having tied it in a packet with a cloth, one should carefully sweat it with lime juice for three *yāmas*; afterwards, it should be washed with cow's urine.
Then, the wise and excellent practitioner should cook the *dhūrta* fruit placed inside [the vessel] using many *lāvaka*-type *puṭa* applications,
like a sun-gem;
there is no doubt that it becomes bound and equal to Śiva.
(The Binding of Mercury by Silver): One should indeed grind the mercury with silver weighing one-eighth part;
the wise practitioner should then form a paste using the fresh juice of *cāṅgerī*.
Having formed a pill, one should cook it for three days in *dhūrta* oil,
as well as in *kaṅguṇī* oil and in oil produced from the roots of *karavīra*.
Likewise, with that which arises from nutmeg (*jātīphala*), that which arises from the *vatsanāga* poison, that which arises from *bhṛṅgī*, and indeed that of the ocean-dryer (*samudraśoṣaka*).
The wise physician should cause [the substance] to be cooked even with *devadāru* wood;
afterwards, a very sharp liquor should be administered like a fire of chaff.
For seven days, a mouth [of semen] certainly arises;
one who drinks milk correctly brings about the firmness of the semen, and not otherwise.
(The binding of mercury by means of *tuttha*):

In a very wide iron vessel, having made a basin-like hollow with *tutthaka*, one should pour into it a measured amount of mercury that has undergone the eight purificatory processes (*saṃskāra*). (YRps 2.85)
Having covered it with powdered *tuttha* and filled it with the juice of *nimbuka*,
one should carefully seal the opening of the iron vessel with a lid.
Then, in a windless and secluded place, the physician should leave it for three days;
thereafter, he should wash it many times using a mixture of warm sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
The color of the *sūtaka* (mercury) is seen to be like fresh butter;
having then bound it into a *rasakhoṭa*, one should subject it to sweating for three days with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
Having placed a pill (khoṭa) in the center of a small amount of powdered stone, one should sprinkle it with water; once it has become cool, one should extract it.
In this very manner, one should certainly cook it three times;
it will surely attain hardness, just as the word of the Guru is true.
Then, one should cook even a thousand *dhūrta* fruits;
this will properly produce an upward flow [of breath] and will also cause the stabilization of the vital energy (*vīrya*). (YRps 2.91)
(Through the seed-syllable of the element, there is the binding of mercury:
Having made tin and iron equal, one should heat them in a vajra-crucible;
one should carefully extract the tin thoroughly using intense coals.
In this very manner, one should circulate the tin three times;
for the seed should be the measure of a *śāṇa*, while the mercury should be one *pala*.
One should grind it with the juices of kanyākā for one day and dry it thoroughly;
likewise, the heating of the ball (gola) should be performed over seven days.
The wise practitioner should indeed steam [the substance] for three watches within a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
using the fresh juice of kumārī and the juice of bhṛṅgarāja.
Likewise, it should indeed be subjected to sudation for three days with *bhṛṅgīrasa*;
in this manner, one should place [the medicine] in a glass jar using each individual herb.
Having ground together lime, salt, and *śivā* (myrobalan), one should block the mouth [of the vessel].
A pit measuring three cubits should be dug, and it should be filled with *laddīs*.
In the center, however, one should place a glass flask filled with wine;
situated in the ground, one should later extract it after two months.
One should take the excellent bound mercury, bright and resembling the luster of the moon;
when properly held in the mouth, it makes the body as firm as a vajra.
Free from wrinkles and grey hair, he may approach a hundred women;
for even this mercury bound by means of minerals acts according to the teachings of the Goddess’s scriptures.
This has been correctly revealed by me; no further deliberation is required here.
(The binding of mercury by magnetite):
Mercury, magnetite, and likewise steel, as well as the essence of mica and the essence of pyrite combined with gold. YRps 2.102.
One should grind all these ingredients in equal parts with the juice of *nimbuka* for one day, and thereafter form them into a ball.
One should prepare a baked crucible and place a ball inside its interior;
likewise, [one should add] gojihvā, kākamācī, nirguṇḍī, and dugdhikā.
The physician should repeatedly foment [the patient] with the fresh juice of kumārī, meghanādā, honey, and rock salt.
As long as the *golaka* reaches a state of firmness, it should be subjected to sweating;
when held in the mouth, it undoubtedly destroys old age and death.
Having quickly destroyed all diseases, it certainly stabilizes one's youth.
When worn on the ear, the throat, the hand, or even on the head,
the defects of malevolent spells and the like never occur.
I have thus declared the four kinds of bonds of the illustrious King of Mercury;
those excellent physicians who, knowing the reality, perform these [treatments] in the palaces of kings, they too become worthy of honor.
Thus has been declared this supreme secret of the King of Mercury (Sūtarāja), this jewel obtained from the great ocean of the Rasa-śāstra.
Those experts who are preeminent in all virtues, skilled debaters, and discerning of its wonder, shall wear it upon their hearts and on their beautiful necks.
YRps, Chapter 3:
Now, mercury ash (rasabhasma) is being described by me in accordance with the application of all the scriptures on mercury (*pārada*).
It exists adorned with four colors: white, black, beautiful yellow, and red. (YRps 3.1)
Mercury produced from *darada*:
Well-refined *haṃsapāka-darada*,
having been rubbed with the juice of all types of *nimba* for four fixed watches (*yāma*), is stirred in an equal portion of sour *ghana-rasa*.
Thereafter, O best of physicians, place iron powder— equal in measure to chalk— into the apparatus called the *ḍamaruka*,
rub it with good milk and salt, and prepare the vessel for the divine elixir (*yantrasurodhana*).
One should cook the mercury here gently and evenly with fire for four fixed watches;
one should sprinkle water upon it there, and thus the excellent mercury (sūtaka) from cinnabar (darada) is produced.
Just as by means of the supreme all-purifying [substance], one becomes entirely free from the defects of the sheaths,
so too does that which arises from mercury (darada) become most pure, removing even the many defects.
Indeed, eight *pala* of excellent pure mercury (*vimalasūta*), followed by one *pala* each of *dhātu*, *khaṭī*, *paṭu*, and *kāṅkṣikā*;
and [finally] eight *pala* of purified crystal (*sphaṭika*)—these [ingredients] should be taken in equal portions. (YRps 3.6)
Having kneaded it together with water, and having mixed it with salt and sour liquid,
fashion a crucible for the collection of the risen minerals, and indeed place the poison therein.
Cook that [substance] for twelve hours with fire using the excellent mantra called *ḍamarūka*;
it always removes the depletion of wind, bile, and phlegm, and is the supreme destroyer of all diseases.

The excellent mercury (sūtavara) bestows strength like the powerful elephant-king, grants vision like the eye of the moon, and brings about the amorous play of young women; it is always a giver of happiness.
Indeed, when combined with the essence of *ghanasāra* (camphor), it is said by me to bestow beauty and remove all forms of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

Mercury and sulphur, which remove defects, should then be thoroughly saturated with the juice of *luṅga* and ground into a fine powder on a stone slab for two *praharas*, rubbed by the rays of the sun. (YRps 3.10)

O best of physicians, place two beautiful glass jars connected by an excellent sand-contrivance for three days; apply fire beneath them, and that [substance] will become reddish, with the luster of a lotus.
Indeed, this elixir named Udayabhāskara spontaneously destroys diseases when it is regularly consumed in a dose of three *guñjā* seeds along with honey and *magadhaja* (long pepper).
Even an old man, desiring the practice of amorous play, acts like a youth in sexual union;
indeed, it removes ailments, bestows strength, and imparts a healthy complexion, curing diseases born from the ripening of past karma.
This has been revealed by me, the best of the twice-born, through a thorough investigation of all the treatises on alchemy (*sūtaka*).
Even mercury purified by the alchemist, and even sulphur freed from defects,
should be released into a crucible made of pure iron as fine powder of stainless essence. (YRps 3.14)
When it has been joined with an intense fire of kuśa grass, the mercury itself melts;
then, let it be released therein and stirred with a ladle made of pure metal for a duration of three praharas.

Thereafter, having placed a glass flask [into the apparatus] and heated it with an excellent sand-oven by means of a fire maintained for twenty-four hours, the red juice becomes reduced to ashes at the bottom.
When practiced by a man whose strength has departed, it becomes a restorative for virility, always bestowing happiness.
And that [practice] destroys wrinkles and grey hair; it is the supreme creator of health for one who has lived a hundred autumns.
The physician should take one part of the finest pure mercury-bhasma mixed with four parts of mercury,
and having ground it constantly upon a stone slab, he should make it equal in weight to the fat of a bull.
Having thoroughly ground the dynamite and dried it with the juice of kanyā using the sun's rays,
one should then place the kajjalī of the excellent mercury into a beautiful glass jar.
When two days have passed below, that [fire] becomes ruddy with the luster of a lotus;
it indeed destroys all diseases, acts as fire, bestows strength, and produces supreme radiance.
It destroys eye diseases and produces all kinds of amorous charms;
indeed, that mercury (pārada), when joined with pure naga, removes diseases born from the ripening of karma.
A smooth brick made of soft clay, provided with an excellent cavity on top, should be used;
one should place ten *śāṇas* of the best mercury therein together with the finest *śukapiccha*. (YRps 3.23)
Having filled the entire cavity with the juice extracted from ripe nimba fruits,
one should cover it with an excellent lid and seal it firmly with well-kneaded clay.

Thereafter, having been cooked in a vessel of hen’s feathers by that physician Hupalaka, who was born in the forest and well-versed in the ritual procedures, one partakes of it which possesses the fragrance of the six stainless qualities.

Furthermore, when that excellent mercury, though it makes the body small, is digested a hundredfold, it becomes the supreme maker of iron and the performer of all siddhis; indeed, when it is thoroughly digested, it becomes the maker of gold.
Even mercury, though resembling a parrot’s wing, becomes [malleable] when ground with *khaṭvāṅga* (khaṭvatala);
therefore, prepare a very firm *parpaṭī* tablet, even one fashioned as a cloth-bound *poṭalī*. YRps 3.27.
Smeared above with *nāgarasena* and constantly dried by the rays of the sun,
and likewise seven times with the juice of golden leaves, place it within the hollow of the earth.
Having filled with sand a pit in the earth one cubit deep, two spans long, and twelve finger-breadths wide and very deep, place there a small bundle (poṭṭalī) half that size.
Having filled it above with sand, let that packet be covered with dried cow-dung cakes;
then maintain the fire for twenty-four hours (twelve yāmas), and by that means the *mahārasa-poṭalī* is produced.
Thus has the *rasa-poṭalī* been described by me—strengthening, easy to perform, and bestowing the accomplishment of happiness. (YRps 3.30)
Even sulphur equal in weight to pure mercury, having been thoroughly rubbed upon a stone slab,
should then be dried by the rays of the sun for exactly three days in the juice of *haṃsapādī*. (YRps 3.31)
Then, having placed the soot-like substance (kajjalikā) into a firm, hard pan made of stainless iron,
one should indeed set a well-fashioned crucible (cuḷhikā) measuring one cubit upon it, and place the vessel on top of that.
One should certainly grind the excellent juice with a ladle made of stainless iron;
thereafter, one must indeed maintain a firm fire below for a continuous period of four watches.

When well-cooked, this essence becomes like water; when combined with honey and taken as a bolus, it destroys the multitude of wasting diseases and is the supreme increaser of virility for men. (YRps 3.34)
And it shall destroy wrinkles and grey hair; it is the supreme means for curing all types of skin diseases.
One should place upon the ground a crucible fashioned from soft clay, measuring one finger-breadth in size,
containing the excellent mercury— pure, well-adorned, and rubbed until it resembles a parrot’s wing. (YRps 3.36)
Equal in measure to the mercury, it is placed in a crucible, sealed with a pair of lids,
and subsequently cooked for seven days over a mild fire with the juice of the golden-rooted plant (*kanakamūla*).

Indeed, the auspicious digestion of the best of juices is like barley; then, that king of the best juices, when well-eaten at the break of day, destroys [illness] and conquers the morbid transformations caused by all the *doṣas*.

(Rasaparpaṭī) Two *pala* of excellent mercury, auspicious and beautiful, together with an equal portion of copper, and the fat of a *bali* [buffalo] should be rubbed with clarified butter; when subjected to very mild heat, it melts by itself. (YRps 3.39)

Thereafter, one should place copper and mercury—these three together with the juice—and having thoroughly ground them, quickly cast the mixture into an iron vessel; thereafter, one should add the excellent collyrium produced from mercury.
Then, one should break it apart with an iron ladle; subsequently, it is placed upon a leaf of *mocā*.
That mercury-leaf (*rasaparpaṭī*) becomes most excellent in essence, for it indeed destroys all diseases.
Prepare it with equal parts of the three pungents (kaṭutraya) and two units of black pepper; this will always grant happiness.
It should be administered as a drink combined with *triphalā* and honey;
likewise, one should consume *parpaṭī* in the morning together with the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*).
Combined with *pañcakola*, it removes the disorders of the humors' conjunction;
when eaten together with honey, it destroys all fevers.
Combined with grain-dust and honey, it cuts away all swellings;
or, together with *śyāmā* and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), it conquers *grahaṇī* caused by wind (*vāta*).
Guggulu combined with the three myrobalans (triphalā) destroys vātarakta;
likewise, asafoetida (hiṅgu) combined with puṣkaramūla effectively removes vāta-śūla.
With the three pungents (vyoṣa) or with the juice of kanyā, it destroys diseases caused by phlegm;
with water boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla), it eradicates fever caused by wind (vāta).
One should destroy itching and eruptions with a paste of *vākucī* seeds;
combined with *āruṣkara*, it destroys *sidhma*.
Taken with cow urine as an after-drink, it destroys the disease of hemorrhoids;
likewise, *navamālī*, *arjuna*, *citraka*, and *bhṛṅgarāja* [are effective].
The best of physicians should prepare equal parts of *śālmalī*, the five-fold parts (*pañcāṅga*) of *nimba*, *kalhāra*, *guḍūcī*, and *nirguṇḍī*.
Having reduced all of that to powder, with *parpaṭī* as the after-drink, it undoubtedly destroys the eighteen types of skin diseases; of this there is no doubt.
Parpaṭī and Rasarāja destroy diseases when taken as an after-drink (anupāna);
one should never consume unwholesome food, having regard for the humors (doṣas), the affected tissues (dūṣyas), and other factors.
(Rasaparpaṭī) Then,
with great care, take equal parts of purified mercury and purified sulfur separately; subsequently,
one should rub the mercury with the juice of castor root and likewise with the fresh juice of *adrikarṇī*.

Having ground that mercury with the juice of *kākamācī* and likewise with the juices of pomegranate seeds, it certainly attains purity through a gradual process over four days; this is indeed certain.
Then, indeed, having infused the fragrance with the juices of *mārkava* in an iron vessel,
one should melt it over a fire of jujube wood and dissolve it three times in the juice of *bhṛṅga*.
Then, having ground that kajjalikā, one should melt it in a vessel made of iron;
one should then place it on a plantain leaf and cover it with another leaf.
One should apply cow dung above and below that [herb], roasted with clarified butter from a cow and cooled;
for this *rasaparpaṭī* indeed destroys all diseases born of impurities and defects of the bodily constituents.

When consumed with cumin and asafoetida, this pure-juice *parpaṭī* cures flatulence, colic, and jaundice in women suffering from *gṛhaṇī*, as well as the eight types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and abdominal enlargements (*udara*).
Indeed, this disease-destroying [practice] has been demonstrated by me as well, surely for the benefit of the true physician. (YRps 3.59)
One should thoroughly purify mercury and grind it with the four salts and the three alkalis;
having dried it, one should then grind it again with equal parts of asafoetida, black mustard, and ginger.
One should prepare a crucible with mercury and the juice of a maiden (kumārī), dried by means of liquid heat;
then, having placed a globule of that mercury inside it, one should properly subject it to sudation with sour juice.
This [mercury], having been processed by fire for eight yāmas and subsequently thoroughly rubbed with a liquid consisting of *bhekaparṇī*,
*urubūka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *śṛṅgavera*, and *girikarṇikā*, [is prepared].

It should be rubbed for three days on the smooth surface of a mortar with the juices of *kākamācī*, *javibhaktikā*, and *dhūrtaja*, as well as with the liquid extract of *jayantikā* and the sap of *siṃdhuvāra*.
Having dried each juice separately, one should consume two *raktikās* of it to alleviate disease.
When rubbed with the bile of a crow, a buffalo, and a boar, as well as with the juice of a tortoise,
it becomes even more effective by its qualities and indeed conquers fainting born of the *sannipāta* disorder.
He who indeed performs this constant service here to the noble Sūta attains supreme happiness, endowed with long life, wealth, grain, and righteousness;
he spreads a succession of fame in the world, his mind becomes fixed on Dharma, and at the end, his supreme goal is certain—this is the truth spoken by Śiva.
YRps, Chapter 4:
Now, therefore, I shall explain the purification and killing of the elements;
some [of this] has been experienced by me personally, and some is according to the scriptures. (YRps 4.1)
(The eight metals: Gold and silver are declared to be pure metals;
likewise copper, iron, lead, and tin. (YRps 4.2)
Corroded iron (pūtiloha) is declared by the knower of mercury to be the second;
mixed iron (saṃmiśraloha) is the third, along with Saurāṣṭra, Rīti, and Vartaka.
These eight metallic ores are to be known; thus indeed do the metals come to be.
(Various types of gold):
Gold is to be known as being of two kinds—that produced from mercury and that originating from a mine.
There are three other varieties of gold that have not been mentioned here.
Gold produced from mercury (*rasaja*) arises through the transmutation by mercury; it is beautiful, enriched with fourteen colors, and is supreme for accomplishing all tasks. (YRps 4.5)
When mountains and regions of the earth are being excavated,
the wise perceive the mineral [substance] in certain places; it consists of fourteen types of colors.
When gold becomes mixed with silver or other [metals], it is no longer fit for the purpose of gold; therefore, it must be purified by the best of physicians. (YRps 4.7)
One should indeed fashion the leaves of base-colored gold;
then, one should grind chalk and fine flour with sour gruel (kāñjika).
Then, one should carefully smear the petals with that paste;
a crucible should be made from wild lotuses, not too large in size.
Then, having placed that [substance] in the middle and enclosed it within the crucible, one should ignite the fire;
having thus applied the three crucibles, one should extract the purified gold.
But a physician should not cause pure gold to be purified;
rather, the physician should cause other metals alone to be purified. (YRps 4.11)
Then, one should indeed cast into it a gold leaf that has been heated.
In the juice of Jvālāmukhī, it is completely reduced to ashes by sixty puṭas.
When correctly explained by the Guru, it certainly becomes free from defects; it destroys all diseases—of this there is no doubt to be made. (YRps 4.13)
One should have thin leaves of gold made, so fine that they can be pierced with a needle.
Then, having smeared it with a paste of mercury, ash, and gold, one should let it dry.
Then, one should enclose it in a *saṃpuṭa* and roast it with ten *puṭas*;
it dies, of this there is no doubt, and an incombustible ash is produced.

Taking fine flakes of gold similar to birch bark and coating them with a paste made by grinding together *vajrī* milk, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and vermilion (*hiṅgula*), one should place them inside a crucible and cook them with ten "cock" (*kukkuṭa*) roasts; thus, the gold will certainly become identical in color to red ochre (*raktagairika*). (YRps 4.17)
Mercury that has been killed and bound within a leaf-cup of copper, taken in equal parts,
and cast into molten gold, will become radiant with the luster of golden ash.
One should grind that ash with water from the eastern direction combined with cinnabar for one day, and then place it within a sealed vessel (*saṃpuṭa*).

Folded ten times, the gold becomes like vermilion; there is no doubt in this matter. It certainly effects a coloring [of the body] and the metal; the wise and wealthy person should accomplish this. (YRps 4.19)
This dust produced from gold indeed bestows beauty and always destroys all diseases caused by fate as well as those arising from the three *doṣas*.
The man who practices this for twenty years does not become old, nor do defects arise from the womb, nor those caused by poison, nor indeed those that are adventitious.
Silver is said to be of three kinds: that produced from mines, that which is innate, and that which is artificial;
these are the three varieties described by the ancient masters.
If silver, which is a mineral, is found within a mountain while it is being excavated,
[it is considered] a sahaja (naturally occurring) mineral.
That which arises from the peak of Kailāsa is declared to be the innate (sahaja).
That which is produced from tin through the process of mercury-transmission (*rasavedha*) is considered artificial silver.
(Regarding the examination of pure silver:)
For that silver which, when heated by fire, emerges radiant, is indeed pure gold; it is supreme for performing all tasks.

Indeed, silver that has become impure through contact with copper and other metals is certainly mixed and defective; one should purify that silver by blowing it in a crucible made of ash together with lead. YRps 4.24.
From the state of *tāra*, the wise practitioner should diligently blow upon the *nāga* six times;
for when it is blown upon slowly, it becomes free from defects.
In this very manner, one should always purify silver;
it should be employed in all rites, bestowing all accomplishments.
One part of silver and four parts of mercury should be ground together continuously for one day with the juice of *nimbū* fruit.
From grinding, the powder is certainly produced within a single day;
having placed that inside the crucible, one should put sulphur above and below it.
Having been cooked with effort for one day over a steady fire within a sand-encased apparatus, it should be allowed to reach the state of being cooled to its own natural temperature.
Having ground it together with sour *tāla* on a stone slab,
one should then apply twelve *puṭa* treatments to it.
By this method, silver is certainly and properly killed. One should grind the powder of silver and copper pyrite together with an acid.
With twenty puṭas, that silver certainly becomes ash;
indeed, an excess of puṭas for metals is properly conducive to their excellence.
It produces an excessive redness, while one should indicate whiteness in the case of the *rakta* [channel].
Pure silver, reduced to ash and combined with honey and clarified butter, [possesses medicinal properties].
It also constantly cures diseases of the eyes, as well as those arising from sneezing and those affecting the anus.
It always destroys coughs born of bile, those arising from jaundice and abdominal enlargements, as well as all disorders born of the humors, and chronic loss of appetite.
Copper is also said to be of two kinds: that from Nepal and that born in the lands of the Mlecchas;
scholars have declared that other than the copper from the land of Nepal is the Mleccha variety.
Copper should be purified with lead, or indeed with silver; thereafter, the alchemist must properly perform the process of killing [the metal]. YRps 4.36.
Having performed the killing (*māraṇa*) of copper, one should place the copper leaves within a virgin leaf;
immediately thereafter, one should properly seal them in a crucible known as the "cock" (*kukkuṭa*).
A very pleasing paste of mercury and sulfur should be prepared;
having ground it with neem water, one should smear those leaves with it.
Then, having confined it within the middle of a vessel, one should cook it for four watches;
by that very means, the copper becomes completely freed from the five defects.
With mercury equal in strength to lead and equal [in quantity],
with talaka half of that, and with realgar half of that; YRps 4.40.
The wise physician should prepare a powder resembling collyrium.
Having carefully placed the leaves inside a hollowed-out pair of earthen bowls,
one should place the soot upon them, layer after layer.
One should cook it in the fire for one watch (three hours) inside the belly of a womb-press;
having removed it when it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should grind it finely in a mortar.
One should cause it to be licked mixed with honey, along with appropriate after-drinks.
One should carefully fashion plates of pure copper.
Of that [substance] having equal parts, and of mercury in equal measure, along with fragrance.
Of one part of *tālaka*, half that amount of [mercury], and half that again of *śilā*;
with *lāṅgalī*, *citraka*, *vyoṣa*, *tālamūlī*, and *karañjaka*.
Equal parts of *viṣa*, *śamyāka*, *ativiṣā*, and *saindhava* salt,
with the powder then thoroughly moistened by the juice of *jaṃbīra*.
Having carefully placed all of that in a stone vessel,
the leaves— which are pierceable by a needle and smeared with the mercury— [should be processed].
Having indeed cast it into the midst of lime for exactly seven days,
it should be ground into a powder and combined with honey, clarified butter, and two types of *kaṇā*.
Indeed, a dose of just one *valla* of this auspicious substance called Somanātha, as taught by Somadeva, destroys old age and death. (YRps 4.50)
Pure copper and sulphur in equal parts should first be placed in a vessel;
half the amount of sulphur should be carefully positioned in the middle over the copper, and above that, another half of the sulphur powder. (YRps 4.51)

Having placed a small jar of powder at the mouth of the vessel and likewise applied a coating of rock salt and clay, one should place it on the stove and apply fire; thus, in just three watches (yāmas), it becomes well-cooked.
Having made that very [substance] cooled and free of defects, one should prepare it as a powder and strain it through a piece of cloth;
when properly consumed in the measure of a single *vallī*, it destroys cough, asthma, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders.
One *valla* of copper ash should be taken in the forenoon by the physician’s command.
There is colic arising from transformation, as well as the eightfold pain.
It cures abdominal enlargement, pale edema, abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, liver diseases, and wasting;
it remedies the loss of digestive fire caused by wasting, urinary disorders, and diseases of the *grahaṇī*.
One may conquer various kinds of diseases through different types of after-drinks;
taken together with long pepper and honey, it is the supreme remedy for all humors.
This elixir destroys hemorrhoids, indigestion, fever, and other ailments;
it cures enlargement of the spleen, asthma, and cough, and it eradicates old age and death.
As it was correctly proclaimed by the best of physicians,
iron— consisting of *kānta*, *tīkṣṇavara*, and *muṇḍa*— is of three types in sequence, each subsequent one being progressively inferior in quality and color. (YRps 4.57)
The *kānta* [iron] is said here to be of four types: *romaka*, *bhrāmaka*, *cumbaka*, and *saṃdrāvaka*;
indeed, it is declared by those who know the scriptures and are connoisseurs of mercury that the *saṃdrāvaka* is the most excellent. (YRps 4.58)
(Romaka):
When a mine is being excavated, stones emerge;
the metal that is melted from those stones is called romaka.
(The Magnetizing Stone): A magnetizing stone (*bhrāmaka-upala*) is found on some excellent mountain; the iron produced from that is here called "magnetizing" (*bhrāmaka*).
(The Magnet): On the Vindhya mountain there is a stone that wondrously attracts iron;
it never lets go, just as a devoted follower [never abandons] devotion to Śiva. (YRps 4.61)
(Regarding the liquefier:

That which is obtained with difficulty on the Snowy Mountain and, when touched, causes iron to melt, likewise causes gold and other metals to do so; that indeed is the *kānta* stone, the liquefier. (YRps 4.62)
When the vessel produced from *kānta* is pure, milk boiled within it will not overflow;
likewise, water boiled in it will become equal to the scent of asafoetida. (YRps 4.63)
A drop of oil cast upon water does not spread excessively, nor does it form a film; this is the characteristic of one who is pure and radiant.
A sharp stone is a hundred times more potent than a blunt one; a magnetic stone possesses great qualities exceeding those of the sharp;
and likewise, a magnetizer and a liquefier are said to possess qualities a crore of times greater.
Indeed, all metals such as *kāntaloha* and others, when smeared with rabbit blood and heated seven times, become purified; of this there is no doubt. (Iron:: Purification) YRps 4.66.
Similarly, iron smeared with sea salt and quenched in a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) becomes pure;
this is as true as the word of the Guru.
Having cast iron powder smeared with ghee into an iron pan,
one should stir it with a ladle until it attains the brilliance of the color of fire. (YRps 4.68)
In the same manner, one should cook it five times in a mortar;
thereafter, this iron should indeed be subjected to *puṭa* treatment four times with excellent waters.
When well-refined, it becomes superior to water; of this there is no doubt.
By this method, the accomplishment of all metals should be performed.
When consumed, it cures all diseases and removes grey hair.
(Iron:: Māraṇa) Two palas of iron powder, with equal parts of jaggery and sulphur, [should be prepared]. (YRps 4.71)
Having thoroughly rubbed it in a mortar, one should subject it to *puṭa* roasting twenty times;
indeed, the grinding should be performed first, and the *puṭa* applied afterwards.
By this method, one certainly becomes completely reduced to ashes;
it surely destroys all diseases—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Ten *puṭa* applications should be administered there with the juice of white *punarnavā* leaves; then, a vermilion-like color arises.
Now, another method for the killing of iron is described here:
one should grind mercury equal in weight to the iron powder with the juice of kanyā.
Having formed it into a ball, one should place it in a metal vessel for a long time in the shade;
it dies, of this there is no doubt, for this has been experienced by me myself.
In this matter, a wise man should consume iron-derived ash that is *niruttha* (unprocessed).
Mixed with one *ṭaṅka* each of *vyoṣa*, *vella*, clarified butter, and honey.
It destroys old age, death, and disease, and bestows sons;
it eradicates the ailments in embodied beings caused by the defects of aging.
Tin is said to be of two types: khura and likewise miśra.
(Regarding the physical properties of khura:)
That which is pure, straightforward, and bright is called *khura*.
The hoof is purified when immersed in oil derived from *bhallātaka*.
(Tin: purification of alloys)
Tin is purified by being washed three times in buttermilk mixed with the powder of *punarnavā*, rock salt (*sindhu*), and *viṣa*.
(On the killing [of mercury]):
When a pit has been made upon cow-dung, one should throw powdered tamarind bark into it;
then, one should place a lead disc weighing one karṣa upon that.
Then one should wear the *cakrī* encircled by four times [the usual amount of thread];
thereafter, one should cause the *puṭāgni* fire to be applied using dried cow-dung.
Having extracted [the mercury] while it is cool to the touch, one should employ it in all ritual operations;
by this method, one will certainly kill the remaining uncooked [mercury].
Now, another method will be described by me here and now:
one should have leaves of pure *baṅga* (tin) made that are exactly equal [in size].
Goat dung is equal to that; likewise, turmeric is powdered.
Then, one should prepare a square pit, one cubit in measure and slightly deep.
The physician should constantly fill half [of the pit] with dried cow-dung cakes,
and then cover the pit with a cloth made of hemp.
One should place the previously prepared powder upon that,
and then arrange equal leaves all around on top of it.
Having carefully covered it with powder, one should then fill it with dried cow dung;
one should properly roast it with fire and, once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body parts, extract it.
Thereafter, one should grind dead *baṅga* with *pūra* water;
one should then mix an equal portion of *rasasindūra* with this.
Having ground it very finely in a mortar,
one should place it in a glass flask and cook it by means of fire for a duration of sixteen *yāmas*.
Tin that has been killed with golden luster becomes mercury-tin (rasavaṅgaka).
Bengal quince (baṅga) increases wind (vāta), is dry (rūkṣa), bitter (tikta), and destroys urinary disorders;
it indeed destroys fat, worms, and diseases, and removes the defects of phlegm (kapha) and poisons.
It quickly removes all diseases, bestows power, and is superior in its qualities.
Having observed the strength of the disease, one should administer a mere *vallaka* dose;
it destroys eighty diseases born of wind (*vāta*) as well as twenty types of urinary disorders (*meha*) by the mere act of consumption, with each successive seven-day cycle— there is no other way.
Tin (mṛta-vaṅga) is said to increase wind (vāta), is dry (rūkṣa), and destroys urinary disorders (meha).
For it destroys worms, obesity, and disease, and removes the defects of phlegm and poisons.
When cut, [lead] that is black, heavy, unctuous, melting quickly, and brilliant is of good quality.
The serpent is beneficial when it is black in color externally and pure; otherwise, it is harmful.
One should dissolve lead into the juice of *sinduvāra* and *haridrā*;
thus the lead becomes purified and will not cause fainting, eruptions, or other such ailments.
One should have the leaves of pure *nāga* made together with their stalks;
one should also grind the stone for a full watch (*yāma*) with the juice of *vāsā*. (YRps 4.97)
One should smear the leaves with that [substance] and then place them in a sealed vessel (*saṃpuṭaka*).
The wise one should cook them using the *vārāha* method with a fire as hot as a donkey’s.
When this is done three times, the ash of the serpent (*nāgabhasma*) is produced.
Now, there is another method for the killing of a *nāga*:
when the *nāga* has been liquefied in an iron vessel, one should perform the rubbing. (YRps 4.99)

With effort, one should properly kindle a *haṭha* fire beneath [the vessel] using four types of fuel and roots made of *palāśa*; it certainly dies [as a solid], and a powder with a reddish luster is produced, which should be employed in all ritual applications. (YRps 4.100)
It always brings about the destruction of disease in all undertakings;
the killing of the *nāga* has been proclaimed in many ways by many wise men. (YRps 4.101)
In every respect, there is no death for the elephant-driver Sūta nor for Śambhu.
Lead [possesses medicinal properties] for urinary disorders, diseases born of Vāta, and ailments such as *dhanurvāta*.
It undoubtedly destroys the twenty diseases born of phlegm as well; of this there is no doubt.
Brass is said to be of two types: *rītikā* and *kākatuṇḍikā*.
(*Rītikā*:: Examination)
But when heated and cast into water with husks, the brass becomes white in color.
When that black [substance] is placed in fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), it is known as *kākatuṇḍikā*. (Examination of *kākatuṇḍī*) YRps 4.105.
If it has a yellowish luster, is soft, heavy, substantial, and golden-hued, it is of good quality.
But that which has smooth limbs, is very glossy, and auspicious, is called *rīti*.
Foul-smelling or putrid-smelling, rough to the touch, and pale;
A style that is harsh, lacking in restraint, and violent is not desired in alchemy.
And brass, when heated and diligently cast into the juice of *nirguṇḍī* five times, attains purification instantly. (YRps 4.108)
The copper leaves should be smeared with mercury that has been thoroughly rubbed together with realgar, orpiment, and rock salt; then they should be subjected to the *puṭa* process eight times.
They immediately turn to ashes; therefore, they should be employed in alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Brass (*rītikā*):
[the medicinal properties of] its dross (*mṛta*).
Rītikā (brass) is considered to cure hemorrhagic disorders, be parching, and destroy worms.
(Brass:: kākatuṇḍikā: :
dead metal::)
Kākatuṇḍā is considered to have medicinal properties that cure leprosy (kuṣṭha), possess a hot potency (uṣṇavīrya), and are laxative (sarā).
When one part of the finest tin is combined with four parts of copper,
the excellent *kāṃsya* alloy is produced; that which originates from Saurāṣṭra is auspicious.
Heated bell-metal is purified by being placed in cow's urine for seven cycles.
(Bell-metal:: Killing)
It is killed by five *puṭa* applications with yellow orpiment and sulfur.
