Melted bronze (*mṛtakāṃsya*) removes wind disorders and destroys urinary diseases (*prameha*).
Indeed, all food whatsoever served in a pure vessel made of bell-metal becomes wholesome,
provided it is not sour and is free from ghee, leafy vegetables, and the like.
That which is produced from iron, bronze, copper, and tin is called vartaloha.
That very thing is designated as *viḍaloha* by the learned.
(Vartaloha:: Purification) When properly cast into horse urine while molten, it attains purity.
(Vartaloha:: Killing)
Round iron is killed when processed with *gandhatāla*.
(Vartaloha:
Mortuary;
medicinal properties)
Sour [taste] removes phlegm and bile, stimulates the appetite, and likewise destroys worms;
it pacifies diseases of the eyes and eradicates diseases of the throat.
Indeed, everything placed in that vessel is wholesome; it is supreme for removing all defects.
Except for alkaline and acidic substances, it produces digestive fire and is the best of digestives.
Indeed, I have declared only the purificatory rites that bring about death, along with their respective merits and defects;
having carefully examined other extensive treatises, this has been correctly composed.
Yoginī-hṛdaya-rahasya, Chapter 5: Now, therefore,
I shall proclaim the great rasas according to their predominance of qualities,
as well as their names, groups, potencies, and their respective attributes.
(The great essences are:
gaganam, tāpyam, vaikrāntam, and likewise vimalam; then rasakam, that which is produced from stone (śailasaṃbhūtam), rājāvartaka, and sasyakam.
These eight great essences have been proclaimed by the alchemists.
I shall now describe, in its proper sequence, the sky which is of four kinds:
white, red, yellow, and black, which is most beautiful. (YRps 5.3)
White [mercury] is suitable for white rites; red and yellow indeed produce yellow results;
black cloud-like mercury is always the supreme destroyer of all diseases.
Vajra, Pināka, Nāga, and Maṇḍūka are thus designated;
according to this method, sixteen varieties are said to exist here. (YRps 5.5)
Among all types of clouds, the *vajra* cloud alone is always the best;
for the remaining three clouds indeed produce terrible diseases.
Therefore, they should be constantly avoided with effort by skilled physicians.
(Vajra:: Examination) A diamond-like [substance], when heated in fire, shall not undergo any alteration whatsoever;
when consumed, it destroys death and makes the body possess the luster of a diamond. (YRps 5.7)
The *pināka* stone, when heated in fire, sheds a multitude of scales;
yet, if used for one month, it effectively produces worms and leprosy. (YRps 5.8)
When nāgābhra is properly smelted, it certainly manifests its power like a nāga.
(The medicinal properties of nāga:)
When practiced [in that manner], it brings about the onset of the disease of consumption (kṣayaroga).
Just as the hālāhala poison, once drunk, certainly kills, so too does this [practice] called Nāgābhra; thus the excellent physician declares. (YRps 5.10)
When heated constantly, it indeed produces the "frog-cloud"; for a moment it does not remain in the fire, possessing a gait like that of a frog. (Maṇḍūkaparīkṣā 5.11)
Indeed, those who know the nature of mercury have stated that the "frog-cloud" (maṇḍūkābhra) must not be used.
One should steam the mica for one day with sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
and subsequently [heat it] over fire in a decoction of *kulattha* beans, or in buttermilk, or in urine. (YRps 5.13)
When heated, the mica (*abhra*) becomes free of defects and certainly attains purity;
likewise, it should be thoroughly heated in fire and sprinkled [with liquids] seven times. (YRps 5.14)
In *kāñjika* as well, it certainly becomes free from defects when processed with mica;
likewise in a decoction of *varā*, in cow’s milk, and similarly in cow’s urine;
it also becomes devoid of defects through the juice of *mārkava*.
Then, having made a fine powder of the mica and ground it with the juices of *haṃsapadī*,
one should form it into a disc-like shape, dry it, and administer half a *gajapippalī* [weight].
Then, having applied six coatings, one should again likewise apply punarnavā; [the mercury] is to be thoroughly rubbed with its juice, along with an equal portion of mica and ṭaṅkaṇa.
Furthermore, having formed it into a ball, one should indeed roast it seven times with the juice of *taṇḍulīya* and likewise with the juice of *vāsā*.
One should seal it for seven cycles and apply the "elephant-half" (*gajārdhaka*) dose;
by this procedure, the mica (*abhra*) is killed without a doubt.
It becomes perfectly free of its white luster (*candrikā*) and takes on the appearance of vermilion (*siṃdūra*).
Iron pyrites (*dhānyābhra*) processed with the juice of *kāsamarda* is auspiciously cooked;
after being subjected to this a hundred times, it is killed—of this there is no need for doubt. (YRps 5.20)
In this same way, having ground the mica together with *ṭaṅkaṇa* and the juice of *mustā* as well as the juice of the roots of *taṇḍulīya*,
one should then form it into the shape of a disc.
When cooked in sixty layers, it becomes like vermilion;
the mica (abhraka) certainly arises as a destroyer of diseases such as leprosy and consumption.
(Regarding the killing of mercury: With the juices of betel leaves, the bark of the root of the banyan tree, as well as with vṛṣā, matsyādanī, matsyākṣī, and punarbhū; YRps 5.23.
When ground and compressed at the root of a banyan tree,
it becomes the color of vermilion by the twentieth compression.
Becoming increasingly subtle with each immersion in water, it becomes brilliantly radiant with a red color;
through many cycles of heating (*puṭa*), it also becomes a remover of all diseases.
The wise should always properly consume purified *vajrābhraka* (diamond-like mica).
For the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair, and for the firmness of embodied beings.

Abhraka (mica) should always be used; it removes all diseases, pacifies the three doṣas, and kindles the digestive fire. It increases virility and retention, cures ailments such as urinary calculi, wards off possession by spirits and insanity, restores memory, destroys swellings and maladies, instantly augments vital strength, and alleviates fever.
Just as poison, a thunderbolt, a weapon, or fire are life-taking,
so too is mica when it is consumed in conjunction with moonlight in its qualities.
Having added one-fourth part of *ṭaṅkaṇa* and rubbed it with the juice of *musallī*,
when heated in a crucible furnace (*koṣṭhikāyantra*), it is produced in the form of essence (*sattva*). (YRps 5.29)
Having ground it in a mortar, the wise one should reduce it to a fine powder;
filtered through a piece of cloth, it should then be thoroughly saturated with clarified butter.
It should indeed be roasted ten times in an iron pan until it reaches the color of fire; having ground it, one should roast it again.
Having ground [the substance] until it resembles a parrot’s wing, one should then process it twenty times with a decoction of *vaṭa* root and with those known as "hog-juices" (*śūkara-rasa*).
O best of physicians, let the wise man likewise prepare the excellent *kaṣāya* by thoroughly saturating it with *nīlī*, *guñjā*, *varā*, and *pathyā* along with *ūlaka*. (YRps 5.33)
The wise man should consume it when thoroughly dried; it is the supreme remover of all diseases.
There is no alchemical elixir (rasāyana) higher than the essence of mica (abhrasattva), none more excellent. (YRps 5.34)
If one should cook it a hundred times with a fierce fire,
then that mercury-like *abhra* becomes supreme for the purpose of transforming the body and [producing] iron.
Then, having prepared thirty-two palas of grain-cloud mica (*dhānyābhraka*),
[one should add] lac, guñjā, small fish, borax, and sheep's milk. (YRps 5.36)
One should prepare all these ingredients in equal parts: mustard seeds, drumstick plant, oil-cake, rock salt, deer horn, and honey.
