Kaṅkuṣṭha is bitter, pungent, and hot in potency; it especially acts as a purgative.
Those ancient masters learned in the scriptures declare it to be supreme for relieving pain in the rectum, abdominal tumors, ulcers, colic, and heart disease.
The extraction of the essence (*sattva*) has not been mentioned [for kaṅkuṣṭha], because it is indeed composed of essence itself.
One should consume this [kaṅkuṣṭha] in the measure of a barley grain for the purpose of purging; of this there is no doubt. (YRps 6.58)
Once purgation has occurred, it destroys fever in an instant;
likewise, when consumed together with betel leaf, it will certainly induce evacuation.
The wise man should repeatedly drink a decoction of *babbūla* root combined with *saubhāgyā* and cumin; he shall conquer poison born of *kaṅkuṣṭha*.
Kāsīsa is of two types:

the first is indeed *saikata* (sandy), and the other is called *puṣpa* (flower-like). It is alkaline and acidic, heavy, removes poison, has a smoky color, is hot in potency (*vīrya*), and imparts a red tint (*rāga*).
(This refers to *vālukākāsīsa*.)

It possesses medicinal properties that destroy leucoderma and dyes the face and hair; that which is found on its sandy banks is the first type, while the other is called *puṣpa*. Endowed with these qualities, it should always be used as it removes diseases.
Flower-named kāsīsa is well known as a destroyer of eye diseases.
It is hot in potency, astringent and sour, an antidote to poison, and a destroyer of phlegm;
it heals wounds, cures consumption, and is supreme for dyeing cloth.
(Refining Kāsīsa: When steamed in the juice of Bhṛṅgarāja, kāsīsa indeed becomes pure. (Precipitating the essence of Kāsīsa:)
One should extract the essence from this as well, just as one extracts the essence of *saurāṣṭrī*.
Take equal parts of iron sulfate (kāsīsa) and the ash of magnetite (kānta),
combined with chebulic myrobalan (varā) and embelia (viḍaṅga), and take it in the morning, saturated with ghee and honey. (YRps 6.65)
When consumed, it swiftly destroys anemia and consumption (pāṇḍu-yakṣman),
as well as splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, pain in the anus, and all forms of dysuria without exception.

When practiced according to the procedure for *rasāyana*, it destroys all diseases, kindles the digestive fire, and eliminates wrinkles and graying hair; it undoubtedly cures diseases arising from undigested food (*āmājīrṇa*). (YRps 6.67)
The salt known as *navasāra*, which is also designated by the names *uddiṣṭa* and *cullikā*, has been mentioned.
Navasāra is said to be a flux for metals as well as a means for the digestion of mercury.
It quickly kindles the digestive fire, removes diseases of the abdominal tumors and spleen,
properly digests the flesh and other [tissues], and brings about the digestion of what has been eaten.
Regarding the examination of the cowrie shell (*varāṭikā*):
that yellow cowrie shell which measures one and a half *niṣkas* is declared by the wise to be the best; indeed, one weighing a *ṭaṅka* is considered middling.
That which is said to weigh three-quarters of a ṭaṅka-bhāra is called the *kaniṣṭhikā*.
In alchemy and rejuvenation therapy, it is said to cure colic resulting from indigestion and other such ailments.
It is considered to destroy disorders of the *grahaṇī* and wasting diseases (*kṣaya*), to be hot in potency, and to stimulate the digestive fire.
It is aphrodisiac, removes the [three] humors, is beneficial for the eyes, and destroys phlegm and wind;
it is praised for the digestion of mercury and is always beneficial when placed within *biḍa* salt.
The large cowrie shell is said to be heavy and a destroyer of phlegm and bile; indeed,
when steamed with fermented rice water (*āranāla*) for one watch (*yāma*), it attains purification.
Cinnabar is of two types: that called Śukatuṇḍa and another known as Haṃsapāka.
(Śukatuṇḍa:)
The blacksmith is said to be the first [of those with physical properties]; he is called one of inferior character.
Having the luster of coral and rich in needles, the *haṃsapāka* is the best.
Cinnabar (hiṅgula), which is an excellent elixir (rasāyana), stimulates digestion and destroys all the bodily humors (doṣas).
Mercury extracted from cinnabar is directly praised for removing all diseases when used in the process of liquefaction (*drāvaṇa*),
just as the king of metals (*rasarāja*) is processed by means of sixfold sulfur.
Cinnabar extracted from Darada becomes endowed with such qualities when it has been sweated within pieces of *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourd using the juice of *lakucha*.
Once purified, he is born; one should employ him in all tasks.
(Gairika: Subtypes) One is stone-gairika, and the second is gold-gairika. (Stone-gairika:)
Regarding its physical properties, it is said that *pāṣāṇagairika* is hard and copper-colored.
Gold ochre (svarṇagairika): it is extremely red, unctuous, and smooth.
Gold ochre is sweet, bitter, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, astringent, and a subduer of blood-bile (raktapitta).
Golden ochre (svarṇagairika) cures hiccup, vomiting, and poison, and it also destroys [excessive] blood;
[so too does] litharge (pāṣāṇagairika).
And there is another, stone-gairika, which is inferior in qualities to the former.
Gairika, when processed with cow's milk, attains purity.
(Regarding the extraction of the essence of gairika:)
Indeed, Nandin has proclaimed that red ochre (gairika) is the form of the quality of mobility (sattva).
The placenta of the fire-crocodile was cast out by the ocean;
dried up by the heat of the sun, it is known as *agnijāra* (fire-born). (YRps 6.83)
Agnijāra pacifies the three doṣas, is astringent, and is supreme in curing dhanurvāta.
It is known as the supreme enhancer of the potency of the rasa and the catalyst for its digestion.
On the Great Mountain, a red-colored liquid situated within a rock oozed out;
dried by the heat of the sun, it became known as *girisindūra*.
Girisindūra binds mercury, acts as a purgative, and likewise pacifies the three doṣas.
Dehalohakara is said to be the leader [of the group], while Girisindūra is proclaimed [as another].
In the land of Gurjara, on the side of Mount Arbuda, there is a place named Udāraśṛṅgaka, which is yellowish in color and possesses a lake. (YRps 6.87)
The *nāgasatva* (medicinal substance from the *udāraśṛṅga*) removes defects of the male organ and cures disorders of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
It properly binds the vital essence (rasa) and is the supreme means for coloring the beard.
All common rasas, when processed three times with the juice of the citron (*bījapūra*) and dried, become free from defects. (YRps 6.89)
Indeed, *biḍa* salt is said to be likewise the supreme remover of all the *doṣas*.
YRps, Chapter 7 (The Nine Jewels):
Ruby, pearl, coral, emerald, and topaz;
Vajra, blue sapphire, gomeda, and vaiḍūrya, indeed, in that order.
A gem endowed with excellent species and qualities bestows the accomplishment of all aims,
whether for the purpose of giving, as an elixir, for wearing, or for the worship of deities.
The first [type] is declared to be the most excellent, known as *padmarāga* (ruby);
the second is *nīlagandhi*.
The second should be blue-scented, dense, red, and very beautiful.

(Ruby Examination) A ruby that possesses great lotus-like luster, is glossy, transparent, heavy, and brilliant; and which is even, circular or oval in shape, and well-proportioned in its body, is considered the best. YRps 7.4.
(Nīlagandhi:
physical properties) Arisen from the waters of the Gaṅgā, it has a dark interior and a reddish-brown luster.
That which has a luster like a ruby and the fragrance of sapphire is called *nīlagandhi*.
A ruby is considered of poor quality if it is of eight types: perforated, dirty, or light.
Harsh, flattened, crooked, subtle, and likewise indistinct.
It is highly stimulating, most aphrodisiac, dry, dispels wind, and removes the pain caused by physical exertion;
it is the supreme destroyer of the three defects such as possession by spirits, always most suitable for kings, and highly praised. (YRps 7.7)
A pearl that is pleasing, white, radiant, stainless, round, and known for its watery luster is said to be of excellent quality.
If there is heaviness in terms of weight and it is smooth, and if it is characterized by these marks as being large, then that [mercury] is pure.
If a pearl has rough surfaces, lacks luster, is dark-brownish or copper-colored, half-white, and knotted;
That which has the appearance of an alkaline substance, that which is produced from stone, that which is double, and that which is afflicted by defects—these must be rejected in every respect.

When used at all times, it destroys cough, asthma, weak digestion, and consumption; it is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and removes bile; it likewise cures diseases such as burning sensations, phlegm, insanity, and wind disorders. (YRps 7.10)
Glossy, thick, with the luster of a ripe bimba fruit, round, long, free of blemishes, and not overly elongated— such is coral of excellent quality.
Coral is declared by the wise to be of seven kinds; when free from defects, it is recommended for all undertakings.
Coral that is rough, white, scarred, greyish, lacking weight, and having the color of copper is of poor quality.
That which is possessed of defects and covered with hollows is not desired by the wise for either consumption or wearing.

Coral destroys bile and blood disorders, and likewise cures diseases such as asthma and cough, as well as difficult-to-overcome poisons; it subdues possession by spirits, insanity, and eye diseases, and immediately acts as a digestive stimulant and a carminative. (YRps 7.13)
An emerald that is glossy, radiant, the color of young grass, pure in its parts, heavy, and possessed of luster;
These seven qualities have been declared; they are indeed praised for giving, eating, and wearing [the substance].
Blue, white, rough, dark and coarse, crooked, black, cracked, and lacking in weight— [these are the characteristics of] an inferior emerald.
The toxic *tārkṣya* (serpent-venom) should be employed as medicine using emerald; it cures cough, asthma, *sannipāta*, and weak digestion.
It destroys swelling, colic, burning pain, disease, poison, hemorrhoids, and anemia.
(Puṣparāga:
Examination:
Good Quality)
A topaz that is transparent, coarse, heavy, and glossy, with a color like the *karṇikāra* flower,
and which is straight, smooth, and delicate— by these characteristics, a topaz is auspicious.
(Puṣparāga:
Examination:
Poor Quality)

A topaz that is rough, yellow, harsh, dark, pale, or reddish-brown like a monkey; one that is flawed, lusterless, or devoid of water—such a stone should not be worn, nor indeed should it be given to the twice-born.
Puṣparāga (topaz) destroys skin diseases, vomiting, phlegm, and wind; it is especially recommended for those with weak digestion.
It is digestive and carminative during burning sensations and difficult digestion; therefore, it should be used by people at all times.
Among all gems, the diamond (*vajra*) is always the most excellent; indeed, it is of various kinds and is the most precious in value.
It is of three types—male, female, and neuter—and I shall describe their qualities in brief. (YRps 7.20)
It has been taught that among these, each preceding one is superior in terms of substance, potency, post-digestive effect, and specific action;
their colors, origins, and eightfold classifications are now described according to the scriptures and their relative degrees of excellence.
Indeed, the four colors—white and the others—are said by the wise to exist in all gems;
these castes (jātayaḥ) are indeed the [social] classes (varṇāḥ), corresponding respectively to the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
That which is called the male-vajra has eight edges and six corners, and is equal to a rainbow.
If there should be eight plows, it would indeed be radiant; it is foremost, excellent, and the remover of all defects.
If the female-vajra is of such a nature, it is indeed somewhat circular, yet somewhat flat and rough.
The third [type] is said to have a blunt tip, to be circular, and to be slightly deficient. YRps 7.24.
Whether it be a woman, a man, one who is neither woman nor man, or that which is the *vajra*—whatever is to be joined, that should be applied to women, to men, and even to eunuchs.
Indeed, by way of reversal, that fruit is not given at all; or rather, the *vajra* would grant that fruit except for the man.

The same applies to color: it is prescribed that the vajra of whichever color should be made beautiful in that very color. And this principle has been correctly taught by Bhairava for all categories of gems whatsoever.
A *vajra* that has been heated until it reaches the state of *yāma* attains purification here in water boiled with *kulattha* beans;
likewise, a *vajra* that has been processed in boiled *kodrava* grain will certainly become purified. (YRps 7.27)
The *vajra* well-saturated with the blood of bedbugs and dried four times over;
Indeed, having been cooked while situated within a chuchundarī, one should cook it again in a *puṭa* with a boar thirty times in this manner.
Having blown upon it again after it has been blown upon a hundred times, one should indeed immerse it in a decoction of *kulattha* beans;
then, having ground it with a stone slab together with realgar (*manaḥśilā*), one should prepare a pill (*vaṭī*).
Having cast it into a crucible and sealed it with eight layers of forest-stones (*vanopala*), one should heat it for a hundred times;
then, having ground it together with purified mercury, one should blow upon it.
All vajras become as soft as clay, and their ashes will even float upon water;
for Śrī Somadeva, whose word is truth, has correctly described the death of the vajra.
In an iron vessel filled with the juice of *kāsamarda*, smeared with the blood of a bedbug,
and heated, a stone indeed splits apart after being sprinkled with urine for seven days. (YRps 7.32)
Those who know it say that indeed, when the substance known as *vajra* has been heated, it causes death.
[This occurs when] the blue-flaming creepers are rubbed upon its bulbs and dried in the heat until they reach the state of ash. (Vajra: Killing) YRps 7.33.
The diamond (vajra) goes [to dissolution] by the application of its own fire when smeared with powdered earth and *nāgas*;
one should carefully enclose it twenty times in a crucible using either wild cow-dung or [other fuel] in a forced fire (*haṭhāgni*).
Thus, the diamond, endowed with potency, is reduced to ashes; this [process] is indeed to be applied to all [substances], such as mercury and the like.
It is declared to bestow longevity, to be the most potent aphrodisiac, and likewise to uproot the three humors.
For it always effects the binding even of the lord of mercury (rasendraka), is equal to nectar, and destroys old age and death.

Having ground it together with *bhūnāga* mercury and the ash of *vajra* along with an equal amount of gold, and having smelted it, it should be applied even to mercury and other substances; this becomes a perfectly effective elixir (*rasāyana*) in this world. (YRps 7.36)
Having ground together three parts of mercury and one part of dead diamond,
the ash of that diamond, when made into a pill and held in the mouth, brings firmness to the teeth of the twice-born.

(Vajrarasāyana, which bestows the accomplishment of the six qualities: One should take thirty parts of vajra-ash, one part of gold as prescribed, eight parts of silver here, and always an equal portion of mercury. YRps 7.38.
Equal parts of mica-essence and ash, one-fourth part of *tāpyaka* (cinnabar) should be used here;
likewise, eight parts of *vaikrānta* ash and six parts of *bali* (mercury) are to be prepared.
When practiced, it always leads to the perfection of the sixfold policy and brings about the accomplishment of all goals.
(Indranīla: Subtypes) Indranīla, vārinīlaka, śvaityagarbhitam, and also nīlaka;
For it is said by the best of physicians that a sapphire which is light, watery, and hollow is indeed worthless;
however, that blue gem which is endowed with luster and possesses a core of blackness is called *śakranīla* (Indra-blue). (Indranīla: Examination) YRps 7.41.
(Examination of Sapphire: Qualities)
Uniform in luster, glossy in color, heavy, transparent, and possessing a radiant brilliance in its center—
sapphire is said to be "massed" (piṇḍita) when characterized by these seven marks, and it is indeed the most excellent.
(Sapphire:
Examination:
Bad quality = *jalanīla*)
If it is weightless, soft, fragrant with blood, rough in color, fine-textured, and flattened, it is indeed called *vārinīla* by physicians; by these seven characteristics, it should be rejected.
Sapphire is an aphrodisiac, a digestive stimulant, a cure for asthma, a root-eradicator of the three humors, and a destroyer of poison.
This excellent blue [rasāyana] is exceedingly strengthening, cures diseases of foul odor and consumption, and overcomes fever.
Gomedaka is the excellent and praised best of gems; it is declared to possess a hue like that of a cow's urine.
Gomedaka that has a color exactly like very clear cow's urine is indeed said here to be pure.

Radiant, glossy, free of fissures, smooth, having the luster of urine, clear, and even—marked by these characteristics, it is indeed superior; this [stone] should be employed in all therapeutic procedures.
Lacking luster, flattened, devoid of radiance, rough, small, and covered with a pale-red hue.
Or if it is weightless, or associated with a yellowish hue, such a gomedaka is not the best for us.
Gomedaka is declared to remove bile, destroy anemia and consumption, and eliminate phlegm;
it is digestive, carminative, appetizing, and an extreme awakener of the intellect. (YRps 7.48)
(Examination of the Quality of Lapis Lazuli)
For the lapis lazuli is indeed clear and even, dark-blue and bright, heavy and translucent;
it displays three pure white lines resembling the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). (YRps 7.49)
(Examination of Vaidūrya:
Inferior Quality)
The surface is rough, light, and uneven, and its luster always appears like dark water;
with a red interior like that of an upper garment, this lapis lazuli is not beautiful at all.
Vaiḍūrya (lapis lazuli) pacifies raktapitta, increases the intellect, and acts as a digestive stimulant.
The wise man should always wear this [amulet], which brings about the purification of the impurities of bile-disease and bestows happiness.
(Defects in all gems):
Scratches, spots, as well as lines, fear, and internal flaws caused by water—these five defects are said by the Lords of Sages to be common to all gems. (YRps 7.52)
And whatever defects arise from the soil or water all completely dissolve away in all the gems.

And hear now their purification as spoken by Bhairava, so that indeed there may be the destruction of defects: (Jewel:: Purification) A ruby is purified by acid; a pearl [is purified] by the fresh juice of *jayantikā*.
Indeed, coral is purified by all types of alkaline substances, and Tārkṣya (emerald) attains purity through cow’s milk;
Puṣparāga is purified by acidic liquids, while Vajra (diamond) is indeed purified when boiled in a decoction of Kaulattha.
Lapis lazuli is purified by being steamed for one watch each with juices made from indigo leaves; emerald with the juice of *rocanā*; and *vaiḍūrya* with the decoction of *uttamā*. YRps 7.56.
(Ratnamāraṇa) One should indeed grind [the gem] together with mercury, sulphur, and mica using the juice of *lakucha*;
even for diamonds, it is certain that after eight *puṭa* applications, they become gem-ash.
As for liquefaction (*drāvaṇa*):
if asafoetida, the five salts, the two alkalies, as well as *cūlikālavaṇa*, *amlavetasa*, and the fruit of ripe *kumbhī* are finely ground; YRps_7.58 //
The root of *citramūlaka*, *rudantikā*, auspicious *jambukī*, and *dravantikā* mixed with water,
along with milk and ghee equal in quantity to the latex of *arka*— all of this should be ground together upon a stone slab.
Having prepared a ball, one should place it among various kinds of jewels;
then, having ground excellent [substances], one should wrap them in birch bark, enclose this within the ball, and surround the ball with urine.
Then, having carefully wrapped the ball with a cloth and placed it in the device called a swing,
one should place it in a sturdy earthen vessel filled with husk-water and mixed with all types of sour substances.
Having extracted that excellent *golaka* from it, one should apply the sweating process for three days;
then, having washed it with acidic water, the liquefaction (*druti*) arising from the jewel is produced.
(The characteristics of liquefaction:
By its color it resembles a gem, and by its luster it becomes light and perfectly sustains the body; it effects the perfect penetration of metal and attains complete union with mercury. YRps 7.63.
They would indeed become perfected when they are properly combined with the group of substances beginning with *hiṅgu*,
having been thoroughly rubbed in a bronze vessel for two watches (six hours) with great effort by the best of physicians.
Indeed, for some person, both [the state of] accomplishment and liquefaction (*druti*) are achieved when Pārvatīśa is truly pleased;
however, as long as the grace of Bhairava has not been attained, he produces bondage that is difficult to overcome.
Among those [states], the rare liquefaction of mercury is the lot of those who possess great misfortune and very little merit.

The qualities of the gems have been described in sequence, as well as their purification, killing, and the extraction of the essence (*satva*) from them; furthermore, the correct liquefaction and the precipitation [of the essence] have been taught. Indeed, the examination of all [the gems], their liquefactions, and their amalgamation within the mercury (*rasa*)—all these operations are fully demonstrated here in this chapter. (YRps 7.66)
In this very [work], the method for various medicinal preparations that instantly destroys multitudes of diseases is correctly described.
Indeed, as the ocean of the nectar of the science of mercury was being churned by me, this compendium of hundreds of calculated mercurial formulations is proclaimed. (YRps 8.1)

The beautiful horn of a deer, finely cut into pieces, should be boiled with the juice of *jalajambuka*. Having sealed it in a vessel, one should cook it on the stove for two *yāmas*; once it has cooled, it should be removed. (Jvarāṅkuśa 1) YRps 8.2.
Then, having added one-eighth part of the three pungents (trikaṭu) and taking a dose of one niṣka, one should consume it in the morning together with betel leaf;
this destroys fever arising from wind (vāta).

(Febrifuge Hook II) Take mercury, sulphur, aconite, *kāravī*, long pepper, and seeds of *dantī*; having increased these in successive order and ground them with the juice of ten *niṃbu* fruits, a pill weighing half a *raktikā* is prepared.
When consumed, this purgative destroys multitudes of fevers; it is a goad that removes fever.
That single, stainless substance, even when processed with water and powder,
is said to remove all cold-related ailments when consumed in a dose of one *raktikā* prior to the first watch of the night.
(Jvarārirasa) Mercury,
zinc, sulphur, realgar, blue vitriol, and borax— all well-purified—
should be taken in equal proportions and ground together for one day with the juice of *kāravella*.
One should indeed smear the interior of a copper vessel with a measure of even half a finger's breadth;
having sealed the mouth of that copper vessel, one should cook it within a sand-yantra.
If grains are scattered above and they burst open, it is declared to be pure;
when consumed, it becomes exceedingly beautiful, an enemy to fever, and a remover of all hosts of fevers.
When consumed daily in a dose of one *māṣa*, together with equal parts of pungent spices and *parṇakhaṇḍa*,
it indeed destroys fevers born of irregular [humors], just as the rising of the sun dispels the darkness.
(Taruṇajvarārirasa):

One should thoroughly rub together one *śāṇa* each of mercury, copper, sulphur, and blue vitriol, along with one *niṣka* of beautiful realgar, using the decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (YRps 8.10)
Having placed it in a hollowed-out *golama* vessel, one should cook it by means of the *puṭapāka* method;
then one should thoroughly saturate it seven times with the juice of *arka* and *vajrī*, and subsequently with decoctions of *dantī*.

When this juice, measuring a single *māṣa*, is consumed mixed with black pepper weighing a *śāṇa*, combined with one and a half *niṣkas* of jaggery, and joined with twelve leaves of *saurasa*; YRps_8.12 //
Whether preceded by cold or preceded by heat, it destroys all fevers, including those recurring every two days;
for this enemy of acute fever pacifies all humors and brings about well-being.
(Jvaraghnī Vaṭī): One part of purified mercury, one part of Ela, Pippalī, and Śreyasī, and one part of sulphur purified by wise men with mustard oil; [these together form] Jvaraghnī Vaṭī. (YRps 8.14)
Having made a powder of one-fourth parts of the fruits of *indravallī*, one should dry it in the heat of the sun;
then, one should saturate this powder with its own juice and make pills equal in size to black gram (*māṣa*).
Having given one [dose] to one who has suddenly developed a fever, the drinking of a decoction of a woman whose limbs have been severed should be administered;
it quickly and thoroughly destroys even intense burning pains arising from the humors (doṣas) or from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta).
(Jvarakṛntanarasa):
Pure mercury, sulphur, and *vatsanābha* [poison] should each be taken in the measure of one *śāṇa*.
One should take three *śāṇas* of *dhūrta* seed, and *hemadugdhā* should be double the amount of all the others. (YRps 8.17)
One should carefully reduce it to a fine powder and administer it properly in a dose of two *guñjā* seeds.
Afflicted by fever, one should consume it with fresh water as an after-drink; this immediately destroys the pain arising from all the *doṣas*. (YRps 8.18)
(Jvarārirasa):
One should take mercury, sulphur, vermilion, and seeds of *Danti*, increasing each ingredient in successive order;
having made them into a powder and rubbed with *Danti* juice, if a dose the size of a *guñjā* seed is consumed, it is the "Fever-Enemy" (*Jvarāri*).
One part of *vatsanābha* [poison], two parts of *ṭaṅkaṇa* [borax] and *dantibīja* [seeds of Croton tiglium],
and three parts of *hiṅgula* [mercuric sulfide]— this "Sun" instantly destroys all pain. (YRps 8.20)
(The flavor of expressing the formal proposition:
One part of pure mercury, two parts of talaka, and four parts of stone;
likewise, one should prepare two parts of copper, or similarly four parts of bhallātaka. (YRps 8.21)
One should saturate it three times with the milky sap of the *arka* plant; having made a powder, one should form it into a ball (*golaka*).
Having placed that ball in the middle of a vessel, one should apply a seal (*mudrā*) using ashes and rock salt (*saindhava*).

In this manner, one should perform the roddhana (blocking) of the smoke; one should apply sudation with chaff over a mild fire. Afterwards, the powder should be processed with water, formed into a ball, and cooked over a mild fire.
Afterwards, one should indeed consume this Rasendra—one *valla* at a time—mixed with powdered sugar.
In the same way, one should destroy burning pain arising from all the humors with black honey alone. YRps 8.25.
(Recipes for curing diarrhea and dysentery): Now, I shall indeed describe the meat-broths that pacify diarrhea;
those which, when consumed regularly, produce immediate results. (YRps 8.26)
(Śaṅkhodararasa):
One should grind equal parts of pure mercury and sulphur for one day with citrons and *unmatta* [datura] plants.
Having filled a conch shell with this powder, it should be placed in a vessel and sealed with great care. (YRps 8.27)

Below that, one should prepare a fire for eight watches; when it is cold, one should add one *karṣa* of poison, and during the heat, three [more], and likewise one should apply three *puṭas* with the juice of the *kanyā* plant.

Valla should be combined with *jīraka*, *bhṛṅgī*, and honey; when consumed, it is effective in cases of *saṃgrahaṇī*, asthma, colic, wind disorders, coughs born of phlegm, hemorrhoids, constipation, and diarrhea. (YRps 8.29)
(Ānandabhairavī Pill):
Take vermilion, mercury, vatsanābha poison, and lac, combined with gold seed;
having made a powder of all these in equal parts, rub it for two *yāmas* with *jambīra* fruits.
Indeed, pills prepared in the measure of a *guñjā* seed, when consumed, destroy diarrhea caused by the derangement of the three humors (*sannipāta*).
(Atisāra-bhairavī-guṭī):
Jātī leaf, devapuṣpa, ginger, kaṅkola, sandalwood, saffron, and pure mākallaka combined with pippalī—all these should indeed be ground into a powder in equal proportions. YRps 8.31.
In this manner, one should prepare a portion of the mercury mixed with ash, and mix in one part of *nāgaphena* (sea-foam).
Having ground everything together in a mortar for one *yāma*, a pill the size of a *valla* should be made to be taken with water.
One should eat it at night and have him drink rice-water; this will destroy all types of diarrhea caused by all the humors.
(Kanakasundararasa):
Take one part each of realgar, borax, cinnabar, sulphur, long pepper, and *vatsanābha* poison;
likewise, take pure seeds of the *dhūrta* plant. Having prepared these, they should be made into a powder. (YRps 8.34)
A single *valla* [weight] consumed in the morning or evening destroys colic, blood disorders, and diarrhea;
or one should feed [the patient] rice with curd mixed with buttermilk, for this likewise overcomes even very severe sluggishness of the digestive fire (*agnimāndya*). (YRps 8.35)
YRps, Chapter 9 (Divyauṣadhī):
The names of the divine medicinal herbs are now being recounted here by me.
There are sixty-four auspicious [plants] that correctly effect the binding of the vital essence (rasabandha):
Somavallī, Sobhā, Ṛkṣa, Somakalā, and Latā. (YRps 9.1)
Bhūpadminī, Gonasā, Uccaṭā, and the creeper Īśvarī; Bhūtakeśī, Kṛṣṇalatā, Laśunī, and Rudantikā;
Vārāhī, Saptapattrā, Nāginī, and likewise Sarpiṇī.
Chattriṇī, Gośṛṅgī, Jyotirnāmnī, Raktikā, Pattravallī, Kākinī, Cāṇḍālī, and Tāmravallikā. (YRps 9.3)
Pītavallī, Vijayā, Mahauṣadhī, Amarī, Latā, Navanītā, Rudravallī, Lambinī, and Bhūmitumbikā.
Gāndharvī, Vyāghrapādī, Gomārī, Triśūlinī,
Tridaṇḍī, Karasī, Bhṛṅgavallī, and likewise Camarikā.
Karavallī, latā, vajrāṅgī, and ciravallī,
as well as rohiṇī, bilvinī, and bhūtaśocanī, are thus described.
Mārkaṇḍī, Karīrī, Akṣarā, Kuṭajā,
Mūlakandāmbuvallī, and Munivallī are thus proclaimed.
The *ghṛtagandhā*, the *nimbuvallī*, the *tilakandā*, the cool *atasī*,
the *bodhavallī* which has the scent of *sattva*, the *kūrmavallī*, and the *mādhavī*.
Viśālā, Mahānāgī, Maṇḍūkī, and Kṣīragandhikā—
these sixty-four are declared to be divine medicinal herbs of great power.
Even by the mere essence of each one [of these herbs], the mercury attains a state of fixation;
mercury prepared with this [mixture] destroys both old age and poverty.
Those [mudrās], endowed with their defining characteristics, were described by Somadeva;
however, for fear of excessive prolixity, they are mentioned here by name alone.
(Rasauṣadhis) Hereafter, the medicinal plants for mercury are described according to the path of the scriptures:
jalotpalā, ciñcikā, jalāpāmārga, and māṃsikā. (YRps 9.12)
Jalakumbhī, Meghanādā, Īśvarī, Aparājitā,
Mālārjunī, Veṇukā, Śikhipādā, and Tiktikā.
Kāśmarī, ativiṣā, samaṅgā, and likewise jālinī; tuṣambukā, durgandhā, pāṣāṇī, and śukanāsikā are thus described.
Vanamālī, vārāhī, gojihvā, and likewise musalī;
paṭolī, śaṭhikā, mūrvā, pāṭalā, and jalamūlakā.
Rasājamārī is said to be śiṃśikā, sitagandhikā,
potakī, viṣaghnī, bṛhatī, and likewise garuḍī.
Tulasī, Vidārī, Mañjiṣṭhā, Citrapālikā,
Jalapippalikā, Bhārgī, Maṇḍūkī, and likewise Uttamā.
Candrodaka, sārivā, hariṇī, kukkuṭā, sarpākṣī, haṃsapādī, and vanakuṣmāṇḍavallikā.
Markasphoṭī, dhanvayāsa, pāgava, sthalasāriṇī, ardhacandrā, hemapuṣpī, mohinī, and vajrakandikā.
Alambuṣā, halinī, rasacitrā, nandinī, vṛścikālī, guḍūcī, vāsā, and śṛṅgī are also mentioned. (YRps 9.20)
It is said that there are sixty-eight medicinal herbs of great power,
prescribed for the killing, digestion, and stabilization of mercury.
(The Great Medicines):
Sixty-eight great medicines are proclaimed according to the science of alchemy (*rasaśāstra*):
*ṛddhi*, *śoṣiṇī*, *adhoguptā*, *śrāvaṇī*, and likewise *sārivā*.
Jyotiṣmatī, tejovatī, rāsnā, bākucī,
bimbikā, viṣāṇikā, aśvagandhā, varṣābhū, and śarapuṣpikā.
Balā, atibalā, nāgabalā, dantī, mahābalā, dravantī, nīlinī, śatapuṣpā, and prasāraṇī. (YRps 9.24)
Varā, śatāvarī, cailā, hapuṣā, sātalā, trivṛt, svarṇakṣīrī, tugā, pṛthvī, viśālā, nalikā, and amalī. (YRps 9.25)
Indravāruṇikā, kāhva, sinduvāra, ajamodikā, trāyamāṇā, asurī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and girikarṇikā. (YRps 9.26)
Dhātakī, kadalī, dūrvā, amlikā, kāsamardikā,
jantupādī, nirguṇḍī, drākṣā, nīlotpala, and śamī.
The coconut, the date palm, the *phalgu*, the *śiṃśī*, and the *mallikā*;
the *vārṣikī*, the *śālmalī*, the *jātī*, and the *yūthikā* of summer and rain.
Kekicūḍā, jagandhā, lakṣmaṇā, and taruṇī—
these are declared to be the sixty-eight great medicinal herbs of mighty power.
(Regarding the accomplished medicinal herbs:
Now I shall describe the accomplished medicinal herbs that excel in mercury:
Devīlatā, Kālavarṇī, Vijayā, Asurī, and Siṃhikā. (YRps 9.30)
Pālāśatilakā, Kṣetrī, Saṃvīrā, Tāmravallikā,
Nāhī, Kanyā, as well as Somarājikā and Ṭuṭumbhaṭī.
Kuberākṣī, gṛdhranakhī, parpaṭī, chidralambikā,
kṣutkārī, dugdhikā, bhṛṃgī, gaṅgeṭī, and śarapuṅkhikā.
The eight creepers are rājaśamī, panasa, jayantī,
viṣakharparikā, avantī, kākāṇḍolā, ambu, and mūlikā.
Siddheśvarī, haṃsapādī, khoṭakā, śṛṅgarīṭikā, adhaḥpuṣpī, the one called madhurā, śṛṅkhalā, and gṛñjanī. (YRps 9.34)
Jārāvalī, Mahārāṣṭrī, Sahadevī, Īśvarī, as well as Kāṣṭhagodhā, Matī, Devagāndhārī, Rajanī, and Iṅgudī.
Palāśinī, Nākulī, Kāmbojikā, and likewise Aśvinī;
Cakravallī, Sarpadaṃṣṭrā, Śallakī, and likewise Rohitā.
Tauvarī, vaṅgajā, rājapadmā, jambīravallikā,
gajapippalikā, bhṛṅgavallī, and arkavallikā.
The *jantukārī*, the *śigru* creeper, the *karavīrā*, the *śivāṭikā*,
the *nārācī*, the *kāñcanī*, and the *ajagandhā* grant the accomplishment of the lord of mercury (*sūtendra*).
Thus, sixty-eight perfected medicinal herbs (siddhauṣadhyaḥ) have been proclaimed, which are superior in their potency;
they accomplish all tasks and bestow perfection upon the body and upon metals.
Now, the instruments will be described by which mercury is constrained;
therefore, the forms of the instruments should be shown according to the scriptures. (YRps 10.1)
(The Mechanical Devices):
The swing, the *palabhalī* device, that which causes upward falling, as well as downward falling, and likewise lateral falling. (YRps 10.2)
The water-wheel (ghaṭīyantra), the internal mechanism (garbhayantra), the brick-water machine (iṣṭikā-jalayantraka),
the mortar (khalva), that called the ḍamaruka, that called the cipiṭa, and that known as the balance (tulā).
The salt [apparatus] known as the *koṣṭhikā*, that known as the *antarālika*,
the incense apparatus (*dhūpayantra*), the navel apparatus (*nābhiyantra*), and likewise the *grasta* apparatus.
Vidyādhara, Kuṇḍaka, and that which is designated as Ḍheki; Somanala, Nigaḍa, Kiṃnara, and the one named Bhairava. (YRps 10.5)
Also the netherworld named Vālukā, that called Bhūdharā,
the secret Sāraṇāyantra, and the Gandhapiṣṭakayantra.
The *kūpīyantra* (well-machine), that called the *pālikā* (pot-machine), likewise the *dīpikāyantra* (lamp-machine),
the *sthālīyantra* (vessel-machine), the *bhasmayantra* (ash-machine), and the *degayantra* (crucible-machine) have been described.
The *ghāṇikāyantra* has been described, as well as that called *haṃsapāka*; thus, thirty-nine instruments have been mentioned here by name. (YRps 10.8)
Now, the crucibles (*mūṣā*) are described in order according to the different types of clay.
Synonyms:
*mūṣā*, *kumudikā*, *kovikā*, and *karahāṭikā* are said [to be names for the same]. (YRps 10.9)
That very [mud] is called *pātinī* and is proclaimed as *vahnimitrā*;
it is the *yogamūṣā*,
consisting of clay mixed with husks and ashes, or clay from an anthill combined with *biḍa*.
The crucible fashioned by her is called the *yogamūṣā*. The *gāramūṣā* is made from *gāra*, *bhūnāga*, *satva*, hemp, and burnt husks.
Clay that has been kneaded with buffalo milk for a period of one fortnight;
a crucible fashioned from that clay is called a *gāramūṣā*.
Take equal parts of cloth, charcoal, and chaff, with four times that amount of clay,
and an equal amount of *bhūnāga* clay; all these should be thoroughly kneaded together.
That excellent crucible has been described, which indeed can withstand the fire for a watch (yāma).
(Varṇamūṣā):

The previously mentioned clay, which has been soaked in the liquid of the red group [of substances], and from which a fine paste mixed with the red group has been made—this is the auspicious crucible (*mūṣikā*). YRps 10.14.
And that crucible, when smeared with *turī*, *puṣpaka*, and lead, should be employed for the enhancement of color; it is called a "color-crucible" (*varṇamūṣā*).
A crucible made of silver, smeared with the white group [of substances], is indeed proclaimed as a silver crucible (*rūpyamūṣā*).
(The Viḍamūṣā):
That crucible which is fashioned from viḍa salt and smeared with viḍa salt itself for the purpose of accomplishing the objectives of alchemy and metallurgy is called the viḍamūṣā. (YRps 10.17)
(Vajramūṣā): A clay mixed with *gāra*, *bhūnāga*, *sattva*, husks,
and *śaṇa* should be kneaded with buffalo milk for three days until it becomes as smooth as fine earth.
Having remained thus for exactly one fortnight,
she then fashioned a crucible, which was smeared with the blood of a bedbug and the juice of *balā*.
For when heated four times, it does not melt even by fire;
it is called the "vajra crucible" for the purpose of melting the vajra.
(YRps 10.21) Having fashioned a tube ten finger-breadths long inside a crucible shaped like an eggplant (*vṛntāka*),
one should have it made as long as a *dhattūra* flower and very firm.
The "vṛntāka-mūṣikā" (eggplant-shaped crucible) should be eight finger-breadths in size and provided with a hole;
by means of this, one should extract the essence from soft materials such as potsherds and the like.
The *gostanamūṣā* is a crucible shaped like a cow’s udder, which is sealed over its opening;
that crucible is known as the *gostanī*, used for the liquefaction and purification of substances. (YRps 10.23)
(The Mallamūṣā):
The mallamūṣā is specified as that which is formed from the union of two mallas;
it is proclaimed for the purpose of steaming mercury-parpaṭikas and similar substances. (YRps 10.24)
(Refractory crucible): A refractory crucible (*pakvamūṣā*) is in the form of a potter’s vessel, which is firm and well-fired;
it is called a refractory crucible because it purifies substances that are difficult to process. (YRps 10.25)
The *mahāmūṣā* is extremely thick and long, and slightly expanded at its opening;
it is called the *mahāmūṣā*, which rapidly purifies substances.
A crucible shaped like a chest (*mañjūṣāmūṣā*), six finger-breadths in height, long, square,
and hollowed out— that is described as the crucible for the killing of mercury. (YRps 10.27)
A crucible that is buried in the ground and covered with sand is known as a *garbhamūṣā*; it serves to bind mercury. (YRps 10.28)
The crucible which is flattened at the base and circular, with a height of eight finger-breadths, is called the *musalā*;
it is beneficial for mercury bound within a wheel. (YRps 10.29)
(Regarding the furnaces: A charcoal furnace (*aṅgārakoṣṭhikā*) is one that measures the span of a king's hand.
It is proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths in width and square in shape.
Then, having encircled it with clay, one should make a pit in a single wall,
with a door one *vitasti* wide and one and a half *vitastis* high, made firm.
A threshold should indeed be constructed at the lower part for the purpose of blowing;
the wall above the upper beam should be one span (prādeśa) in height.
Above that, one should certainly construct a door measuring one span (prādeśa);
having sealed the door with bricks, one should effect a complete closure of the joint.
One should fill that bellows with *kokila* [medicinal substances] and indeed blow it;
one should then place the substance for blowing the *kokila* into the upper opening.
And this is the charcoal furnace for donkeys, used for precipitating the essence.
(Regarding the subterranean chamber: One should dig a firm pit in the ground measuring twelve finger-breadths [in depth];
in its center, one should make a firm circular pit measuring four finger-breadths.
One should firmly place a crucible there upon the central cavity;
having filled the cavity with *kokila* [fuel], one should blow it with a single bellows.
That is the *pātālakoṣṭhikā*, which causes the precipitation of soft-bodied beings.
The crucible should be one span in depth and likewise one span in width;
its lid, moreover, should be provided with many holes on the upper side.
Having filled a pit with charcoal, one should heat it in a crucible;
this is designated as the *gāragoṣṭhī* for the purpose of precipitating the essence (*satva*).
The *tiryakpradhamanakoṣṭhī* is one *vitasti* in height and four *aṅgulas* at its base;
it is called the *tiryakpradhamanā* and is used for the extraction of soft substances.
On the ground, one should indeed dig a square pit two cubits deep;
immediately thereafter, one should fill it with a thousand pieces of dried cow dung.
One should place the medicinal substance in the center, covering it with wild blue lotuses (*vanotpala*),
and then properly ignite the fire with five hundred [of them].
This "Great Casket" has been proclaimed as composed by the author.
(Gajapuṭa):
A square pit measuring one *rājahasta* in size is dug, and the middle of the pit is filled with a thousand wild blue lotuses (*vanotpala*). YRps 10.44.
Then, one should seal that [vessel] filled with the medicine and a mouse;
having placed it in the middle of a pit, one should cast earth upon it.
One should properly kindle a fire below; thus, it becomes a *gajapuṭa*.
In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one *aratni*, it is called the *vārāhapuṭa* (boar-enclosure).
The *kukkuṭapuṭa* (cock-enclosure) [is likewise described].
If one knows a square pit measuring two *vitastis* as the "cock" (*kukkuṭa*) type of enclosure for the preparation of medicinal herbs, [it is effective]. (YRps 10.46)
(With the pigeon-pose): A proper *kapotapuṭa* is said to be formed with eight layers of dried cow dung.
The preparation of the mercury-ash may be done using husks or cow-dung;
a "cow-dung pit" (*govara*) is said to be a sealed crucible (*puṭa*) measuring two *māṇikas*.
(Mṛdbhāṇḍapuṭa):
Having filled a clay vessel with earth, one should place the substance in the middle;
one should ignite a fire from below—this is called the *mṛdbhāṇḍapuṭa*. (YRps 10.49)
In a pit filled with sand (*vālukāpuṭa*), one should place the substance in the middle;
one should diligently apply fire both from above and from below.
That is correctly called a "sand-pouch" by those learned in the scriptures.
Having placed a crucible made of earth within the ground at a depth of two finger-breadths,
one should apply a cover on top; that crucible is called the *bhūdhara* (earth-holder).
A *puṭa* prepared with cow dung or husks, each measuring one *karṣa*, is called a *lāvaka*; it is used for the preparation of soft substances. (YRps 10.52)
Utpala, piṣṭaka, chāṇa, upala, gariṇḍaka,
chagaṇopalasārī, and navāri are the names for dried cow dung.
YRps, Chapter 11:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme wonder regarding the bodily constituents (dhātus),
which has been partly experienced by me myself and partly indeed heard from the scriptures.
Therefore, I shall fully explain that by performing which a person becomes happy.
(The Method for Making Gold) (1):
One should grind together equal parts of *rasaka*, *darada*, *tāpya*, *gagana*,
and *kunaṭī* with the milky sap of red *snuhī* for seven days.
It should indeed be cooked by means of a water-machine for twenty-four yāmas;
with that [liquid], copper, silver, or even lead is to be quickly pierced.
Its paste becomes a thousandfold piercer; of this there is no doubt.
(The Procedure for Making Gold) (2):
One part of mercury is then ground with *vajravallī* in a mortar together with three parts of the fresh juice of *trinemi*. YRps 11.5.
And by means of a red cane-stick, a yellow paste is produced;
it should be added in a sixteenth part to well-purified molten copper.
From this, the most excellent, pure gold of fourteen-fold color is produced.
(The Procedure for Making Gold, 3): Sulphuric gold ore (*suvarṇamākṣika*) should be sweated in sour gruel (*kāñjika*) for three days;
then one should grind it with the juice of *carmaraṅgī* for seven days.
It should be washed with water until it becomes like gold in appearance.

(4) The Procedure for the Preparation of Mercury: One should steam cinnabar from the Romadeśa region with cow’s urine alone in a *dolāyantra* for four watches (*yāmas*); thereafter, it becomes perfectly purified.
Realgar, resembling a lotus, red and very beautiful,
should be heated by means of a swing with the juice of *munipuṣpa*.
One should employ pure [mercury] measuring half a *yāma* in all operations;
likewise, the fluxed mineral salt (*navasāra*) and mercury, once purified, are indeed capable of withstanding fire.
One should grind all these ingredients in equal proportions with the juices of *nimbuka*,
with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, and with the fresh juice of *kumārī*.
This should be rubbed in the heat of the sun and cooked in a water-vessel for three days over a fierce fire; thereafter, one should remove it from that.
One should pierce the silver with a hundredth part [of the mercury]; pure gold is thereby produced.
When there is no separation by water, no further deliberation is required here.
(5) The Procedure for Making Gold: Lead killed with a stone and the fresh juice of *kumārī*,
through the application of twelve *puṭa* cycles, produces lead ash.
One should prepare exactly one hundred packets in this manner using small earthen bowls;
one should then saturate them with the fresh juice of a virgin for seven days.
The sealing (puṭana) should be performed as before, numbering one hundred times;
likewise, if the mercury ash, mica, and orpiment are equal in measure to the lead ash.
One should apply the *puṭa* known as *vārāha* using thirty pieces of cow-dung;
according to this procedure, one should properly administer it one hundred times.
When the three hundred and twelve packets have been prepared in this manner,
they are subsequently placed in a firm glass vessel for thirty-two watches (yāmas).
One should apply sand-fire and, once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, remove it;
that ash should be collected and used to transmute copper and silver.
By this, one becomes pure gold; no deliberation is required here.
This is taught as a practice with visible proof; there is no doubt in this matter.
(6) The Procedure for Making Gold:
Then, one should subject *tāpyaka* to sudation in cow urine, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and *kulattha* pulse for three days; thereafter, one should grind it in an iron vessel.
Having ground it thoroughly with *taptakhala*, one should sprinkle it with the juice of *nimbūka* fruits;
thereafter, one should specifically add rock salt (*saindhava*) in the measure of a fourth part.
One part of *tāpyaka* (pyrite) and three parts of mercury should be prepared;
one should grind them with lime juice and filter them through a clean cloth.
The excellent physician should cause the paste that adheres to the cloth to be taken up;
when this is done two or three times, the mercury will swallow the essence of copper.
The wise one should form a ball from the flour and heat it in a crucible; the beautiful essence of copper (tāpyasattva), resembling an *indragopa* insect, should be extracted.
Even when the gold is of inferior quality,
one should melt down the gold by adding one *valla* of copper and one *valla* of *tutthaka* for every *gadyāṇa*.
One should prepare leaves of that gold and apply an ointment in this manner;
one should also grind *tutthaka* with the juice of *bījapūra*.
Having mixed it with red ochre, one should coat gold leaves and carefully heat them in a mild fire two or three times.
Gold indeed arises with the luster of saffron; there is no doubt about this.
O lords of commentators, act truly according to the word of the Guru.
Both castes increase properly; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
(The Procedure for Making Gold, 7) Pure copper, equal in weight to the powder of *tāpya* (calamine), should be melted and then poured into *lākucī*.
Having reduced the powder of *gandhaka* to the residue of *tāpya* and copper, one should add a *vallaka* of it to [the gold] of inferior age.
By that, an excellence of complexion arises; thus Nandin has correctly spoken the truth out of curiosity. (YRps 11.32)
(8) The Procedure for Making Gold:

Having made a powder of mica, mercury, sulphur, lead, realgar, and pure gold, one should place it in a glass flask and fill it to the top with their own juices or those derived from vegetables. YRps 11.33.
One should apply fire in a crucible known as *lāvaka*; after sixty [applications], the medicinal paste (*kalka*) becomes pure.
Pure silver, when pierced by the *vallaka* [paste] in the measure of one *gadyāṇa*, indeed becomes pure gold.

(9) The Procedure for Making Gold: Lead, which is like an enemy and equal to poison, is processed with the juices of the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*) and the powders of *balivaśa* and mountain minerals, well-burnt in an iron vessel; when bound within a gold-essence by well-prepared portions of snake-mineral (*phaṇibhāga*), this mercury that has conquered the serpent becomes a "lac-piercer" (*lakṣavedhī*).
(10) The Procedure for Making Gold:
One should take two parts of pure copper, two parts of pure gold, and likewise four parts of pure silver. YRps 11.36.
The mercury should be diligently divided into eight parts;
when placed in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā) and heated until melted, it becomes gold.
(11) The Procedure for Making Gold:
Indeed, when cooked in a small crucible by those who have mastered the traditional teachings, gold that has been bound with three parts of powder attains the state of silver. YRps 11.38.
(12) The Procedure for Making Gold: One *pala* of mercury and half a *prastha* of purified sulfur [should be processed] with the juice of *kiṃśuka* leaves or with juices derived from flowers.
One should indeed rub it in the sunlight for a maximum period of six months;
silver is pierced by a sixteenth part [of the additive], of this there is no doubt.
Gold that possesses seven colors is fit for sale in the marketplace.

(The Procedure for Gold-Making, 13): Mercury, sulfur, copper, honey-gold (mākṣika), blue vitriol (tutthaka), as well as zinc (rasaka), cinnabar (darada), golden ochre (svarṇagairika), and navasādara. YRps 11.42.
One should grind together equal parts of sulfur, borax, and mica;
having added half as much *rasaka*, one should seal it within a *vajramūṣā* crucible.
One should cause the seal to be applied in such a way that the smoke does not escape;
indeed, one *tolaka* of gold is produced—of this there is no doubt.
The physician should indeed blow [the bellows] continuously for a duration of exactly four *ghaṭikās*.
(The Procedure for Gold-making, 14):
A ring made from one *gadyāṇa* of gold with very little color [is prepared];
[the ingredients are] *mākṣika*, *rasaka*, *tuttha*, *gairika*, and *navasādara*.
One should prepare two *valla*s each of well-protected sulfur, realgar, and borax, together with the flowers of *kāsamarda*.
Having ground together the urine of a woman, one should smear a ring with it,
along with sorā-alkali, red lead, and borax.
Having placed one part of rock salt and two parts of brick in the middle of a *sthālikā* apparatus, one should position the seal (*mudrikā*) therein.
One should diligently maintain the fire for a period of three watches;
then, having allowed it to cool to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract that seal.
Through friction, the four Vedas indeed increase—of this there is no doubt.
(The Method for Making Gold) (15): Copper that has been drawn from a mine, combined with silver,
along with the powder of *tīkṣṇa* and realgar, should indeed be rubbed with the juice of *kanyā*.
Afterwards, small pills, as fine as *āḍhakī* seeds, should be prepared;
once the substance has been liquefied, these should be sown into it, and all the copper should then be cast in.
Having extracted the silver being refined, one should melt it together with equal amounts of gold;
thus the ten-fold color arises—this is the truth that has been declared.
(16) The Procedure for Making Gold: Lead that has been processed seven times with copper should indeed be processed once more;
with that copper, one should process *rasaka* seven times.
For that copper indeed becomes gold-colored; there is no doubt in this matter.
(17) The Procedure for Making Gold:
One should melt excellent gold in a crucible containing the essence of *bhūnāga* and *sattva*,
repeatedly adding it along with the essence of *tāpya* one hundred times over.
Gold arises resembling a hibiscus flower; there is no doubt about this.
(18) [The Method for Making Gold: In a *gadyāṇa* of ten *varṇas*, that gold which is red is "gold with veins" (*hemavallaka*).
When two *varṇas* increase perfectly, it becomes fit for sale in the marketplace.
(19) [The Procedure for Making Gold] One should grind beautiful *puṣpakāsīsa* in the juice of *arka* leaves; then, one should form a pellet (*cakrikā*) of mercury weighing one *pala*. YRps 11.58.
Wrapped with the previous kalka, one should dry it in the heat of the sun;
thus, twenty *puṭas* should be performed properly using thirty pieces of brick each time.
Silver is pierced by a sixteenth part; there is no doubt about this.
Indeed, it becomes identical in color to the seven metals; there is no doubt about this.
(The Procedure for Making Gold) (20): Two palas of mercury should be prepared, along with four palas of *sumbila*;
a pure and auspicious crystal weighing four *ṭaṅkas* should also be prepared. YRps 11.61.
Having rubbed it for one day with the juice of *vṛścikālī* and with *vārtāka* fruits,
one should then dry everything and place it in a *ḍamaruka* apparatus.
One should first place red ochre and likewise chalk upon it;
having made a pit in the middle of that, one should carefully place fresh [cow dung] in the pit.
A *ṭaṅka* measure should be prepared, and upon that, mercury (*sūtaka*);
indeed, upon the mercury, the essence (*sāra*) as previously described, measuring one *ṭaṅka*.
Having formed the mudrā and dried [the substance], one should afterwards place it on the hearth;
one should apply fire with effort for a duration of sixteen watches (yāmas).
Having removed it while still warm to the touch, one should cause it to be held above;
then, having placed it in a mortar, one should grind it with *vṛścikālī*.
One should place everything in a glass flask and [submerge] the flask in a sand-bath apparatus;
one should maintain the fire for twelve watches (yāmas), and once it has cooled, one should collect [the substance].
Then one should give a *valla* of that [mercury] along with half a *ṭaṅka* of good copper;
this is the application of proven efficacy spoken by Nāthasundara. (YRps 11.68)
(The Method for Silver-making [1]) One *pala* of iron powder, *sumala-kṣāra*, mica,
and *ṭaṅkaṇa* in the measure of one *śāṇa*, indeed with *eraṇḍa* oil; YRps 11.69.
One should rub two pills together, form them into a ball, and then blow upon it with a bellows;
when properly smelted, the metal becomes like mercury.
The wise one should then cause that iron and the *rasaka* to be tripled;
subsequently, the iron and the *rasaka* are melted together in a *vajramūṣā* crucible.
Having removed the remaining iron, one should add a *valla* of copper; thus there will be silver in a *gadyāṇaka*, and that silver [should be added] to pure silver.
In one half-portion, there should be pure silver, free from defects.
(The Procedure for Making Silver, 2):
A piece of *sumala* alkali weighing one *karṣa*, wrapped in human hair, is immersed in molten lead. YRps 11.74.
Having been extinguished twenty-one times in lemon juice,
five *raktikās* [of this substance] are added to one *gadyāṇa* of molten copper.
One should diligently apply a paste, and it becomes the color of silver;
having added four *vallās* of silver to one *gadyāṇa*, one should melt it down.
A beautiful silver is produced—this which has been declared is the truth.
(The Procedure for Silver-making [3]) One should prepare eight *pala*s of conch shell named *sumbala* and grind it for one day, mixed with the juice of *gojihvā*.
One should grind it for one day with the juice of *nimbū*, the juice of *dhūrta*, the juice of *kākamācī*, and indeed the juice of *gṛñjana*.
It should indeed be processed with the milk of the *arka* plant and with castor oil; having formed a pill the size of a barley grain and dried it in the hot sun, [one should use it]. (YRps 11.79)
Having placed [the substance] inside a glass flask, one should seal the mouth of the flask;
having set it in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra), one should cook it for sixteen watches (yāma).
Having removed it once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, that essence which rises upward should be taken;
indeed, a single *gadyāṇa* of that essence, encapsulated within *tāra*, [is the measure].
One *gadyāṇaka* of pure mercury, five *valla*s of *ṭaṅkaṇa*,
and an amount of alkali equal to the mercury— all these should be ground together in one place.
Having formed a pellet from the sap of the *ketakī* flower and dried it,
one should place that pellet within the cavity of a *tāra* (silver) casket.
Thereafter, one should place a beautiful crucible made of copper weighing eight *valla*s inside a pair of earthen saucers (*śarāva*). YRps 11.84.
Having made an equal amount of grain-mercury (dhānyābhra) into a paste with *paṅka*, one should fill a crucible;
by means of a single *vārāha* named *puṭa*, an excellent paste is produced.
One should melt together in one place twelve *valla* of copper, two *valla* of silver, and one *valla* of pure tin.
A wise physician should administer a dose measuring four *guñjās*; thus, the most excellent silver (*tāra*) is produced—this which has been declared is the truth. (YRps 11.87)

(4) The Method for Making Silver: O King, bone-eating *malabhañjana* killed with *tālaka*, mica, poison, mercury, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, when well-purified with the milk of *vajrī* and *bhānu*, becomes a mountain of auspicious silver.

(5) The Procedure for Silver-making: Lead, orpiment, mica, mercury, iron, poison, and borax—when processed in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*) by means of the *traivāra* method, they produce [silver] with the luster of the moon. YRps 11.89.
The rim is one-twelfth part, and the seed-syllable [pedestal] is one-fourth of eight suns (sixteen units);
it is free from all defects such as unevenness in the ground and its parts, as declared by the venerable feet of Śrī Pūjyapāda.

(The Procedure for Silver-making) (6): Three parts of mercury and one part of silver, having been thoroughly rubbed with lime juice and carefully ground into a paste, [should be processed]. YRps 11.91.
One should cause that paste to set with fermented gruel (kāñjika) for three days;
thereafter, one should extract the mercury (sūtaka) into the midst of tin.
One should prepare the processed mercury with that essence of *tāla*;
by means of it, one should carefully pierce molten copper with a sixteenth part [of the mercury].
The preeminent *tāra* arises, resembling the moon and the stars.
(The Procedure for Silver-making) (7): Three parts of mercury and likewise two parts of tin should be ground together with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) for one day. YRps 11.95.
Then, one should crush it with *sumbala* three times the quantity of all [the other ingredients],
and should saturate it for three days with an equal amount of the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*.
Having placed a pill the size of a barley grain, dried by the heat of the sun,
inside a glass flask, one should then apply fire with great care.
One should cook it in a sand-vessel for up to sixteen yāmas;
having removed it once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract the upward-moving essence.
Indeed, by piercing the copper with a needle [made from] a sixteenth part [of mercury],
an excellent silver is produced, fit for sale in the marketplace.
(The Procedure for Silvering) (8): One should diligently grind eight *pala* of *tāla* with mercury weighing two *karṣa* using lime juice for one day. YRps 11.100.
Afterwards, the wise one should indeed massage it with castor oil and cook it for sixteen *yāmas* while situated within a *vālukāyantra*.
Afterward, having extracted the essence, one should crush it for a single day and place it in a glass jar with linseed and sesame oil.
One should cook it in the fire as before and remove it when it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body;
in this very manner, one should perform it once again.

If the essence situated at the bottom of the vessel is always to be taken as excellent, one should undoubtedly perform the transmutation of copper by means of a sixteenth part [of that essence]. (YRps 11.104)
(The procedure for silver-making, 9): One *ṭaṃka* of mercury and twice that amount of salt should be ground in a mortar until the mercury is destroyed [i.e., dissolved]. YRps 11.105.
Make one pure *gadyāṇaka* of copper and one *valla* of tin. Then, when the copper is molten, add salt combined with mercury.
One *māṣa* of mercury should be given along with a fourth part of silver;
that mercury, having been rubbed with the silver, should be cast into a water-wheel (*jalayantraka*).
Therein, silver is produced as thirteenfold; of this there is no doubt.
(The Method for Making Silver, 10): Tin struck with copper, and that copper with silver, should be cooked properly for eight watches; thus the medicinal paste (*kalka*) is produced.
One should give a *valla* of mercury for each *gadyāṇaka*; thus, the mercury is certainly fixed as *baṅga*.
(11) The Method for Silver-making: Having cut cinnabar into pieces measuring three *ṭaṅkas* each,
it should be separately sweated by practitioners using *vajrī* milk in a *dolāyantra*.
One should apply an equal amount of powdered *tāra* (silver) together with an equal amount of *luṅga* juice;
one should cook this slightly over cow-dung fires for twelve *yāmas*.
By that, the mass of the flour-paste becomes firm; thereafter, one should separate the fine powder and add lead equal in measure to a piece of cinnabar (darada).
One should strain [the substance] within a crucible, cool the *khoṭaka*,
place the ash upon the crucible, and blow gently and gradually.
Indeed, silver resembling a pure conch shell shall emerge in the measure of one *niṣka*.
(12) The Procedure for Silver-making: Two *palas* of pure mercury (*sūta*) and two *palas* of *rasaka*,
two *palas* of *tālaka*, and exactly two *mātrās* of *surmila*.
One should place everything inside a crucible and seal its opening with copper;
it should then be cooked properly in a sand-oven for twelve watches (yāmas).
Whatever substance adheres to the mouth of the crucible should be diligently extracted;
one should then cause excellent silver to be produced by means of sixteen-fold transmutation into copper.

(The Method for Making Silver, 13): One *pala* of mercury (*sūtaka*) with the luster of a conch shell and one *pala* of *surmila*, rubbed in castor oil and placed within an excellent crucible; YRps 11.118.
Having covered it with a copper vessel and sealed it very firmly,
one should afterwards place it upon the stove and apply fire very gradually.
Then it should be cooked for one and a half watches; once it has cooled to the temperature of its own body, one should extract it.
Whatever essence adheres to the copper vessel, all of that should be collected. (YRps 11.120)
Smeared with clarified butter and combined with borax, it should be melted in the mouth of a crucible;
indeed, that essence, in a quantity of one ball (vallamātra), should be added to molten copper.
The silver becomes as white as a conch shell; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
(The Method for Making Silver, 14):

One should take equal parts of tin, copper, brass, and bell-metal, and having thus melted and cast them, one should repeatedly wash them seven times in an acidic group of substances; thereafter, they should be added to an equal portion of silver.
Pure silver, indeed called sixteenfold, when properly produced and seen, is not false; this is the truth.
(The Method for Making Silver) (15):
Pure white *sauvīraka* [salt], purified and processed with *viṣamuṣṭi*,
when one *valla* of it is cast into excellent, clear mercury, it becomes a maker of silver.
(The Method for Making Silver, 16):
Somewhere, a substance resembling pure crystal is seen;
it is indeed *surmila* when cooked in an earthen pan combined with the juice of *nimbūka*.
Within the measure of two *ghaṭikās*, the pure paste is produced;
with a measure of sixty-four parts, one should transmute auspicious base metal (*śulvaka*).
It arises as the most excellent *tāra*, free from all defects.
(The Procedure for Silver-making, 17): A crucible made of the seven metals, filled with alkaline ashes produced from the ash of plantain and likewise from apāmārga; YRps 11.128.
Having removed the mercury from the middle, one should fill it again in this same manner;
by this procedure, the second auspicious crucible should be filled.
It should be sealed with effort and placed in a leaf-cup of *govara*.
The mercury attains a bond and becomes like tin in appearance;
it becomes easily fusible and capable of withstanding heating—this indeed has been observed by me. (YRps 11.130)
(On the manufacture of artificial pearls:
Having extracted the eyes of fish and boiled them in milk for one watch (three hours), one should subsequently extract the black specks and grind them. YRps 11.131.
One should first have those [parts] made white with rice;
afterwards, taking brick powder in the hand, one should grind it.
For indeed, pearls are produced; thus have they truly been fashioned by me.
(Producing large pearls from small pearls): One should prepare a pure crucible made of crystal or fire-stone;
then, one should place the small pearls into the juice of *nimbū*. (YRps 11.134)
Within a day and night, all [the ingredients] become like fresh butter;
one should then prepare a smooth pill from that paste.
Afterwards, in that mouse-hole, for two watches during the intense heat, four bronze vessels were placed, situated in the four directions. (YRps 11.136)
One should cause all small [pearls] to fall upon a medium-sized vessel;
thus, the finest pearl, endowed with all excellent qualities, is produced. (YRps 11.137)
(On the manufacture of artificial coral:
Having carefully reduced pure conch-shell to a fine powder, the wise man should then grind half that amount of vermilion (darada). YRps 11.138.
The wise man should grind fresh goat’s milk with that same milk,
fashion a wick, and heat it over cotton seeds.
Having removed it once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, the coral will become radiant.
YRps, Chapter 12 (Vānarī Vaṭī):
Eight *pālikas* of dried *ātmaguptā* fruit, dehusked and cleaned;
Likewise, eight palas of black gram (māṣa) should be ground with water.
Having thoroughly moistened both, one should grind them on a stone slab with saffron,
*kesara*, jasmine petals, and *śatāvarī*.
One should take one karṣa each of the seeds of gokṣura and ikṣu, as well as cloves, black pepper, long pepper, and water chestnut (śṛṅgāṭaka), keeping them separate.
Then, having made a fine powder, one should place it into the previously prepared paste;
afterwards, one should form pills of one *karṣa* each and cook them.
One should immerse the well-prepared [substance] in exactly three *prasthas* of clarified butter;
indeed, one should seal the mouth [of the vessel] with honey for three days, using a quantity equal to that of the clarified butter.
In the morning, one should eat each ball mixed with honey and clarified butter;
thus, for five weeks, one should partake of this sweet diet.
Likewise, one should avoid milk-rice at night, as well as alkaline and sour foods;
even one whose semen is diminished or who is impotent may approach a hundred women.
One without a son obtains a son, and even a eunuch attains virility;
this is a practice whose efficacy is directly perceived—this which has been declared is the truth.
(1) *Śatāvaryādivājīkara-avaleha*:
One should take half a *prastha* each of *śatāvarī* and *kṣīravidārī* separately;
likewise, one *prastha* of the juice from the inner core and roots of the *śālmali* tree, and half an *āḍhaka* of white sugar should be added here. YRps 12.9.
Just as a paste applied with a ladle becomes perfectly cooked when heated by a gentle fire,
one should then add cinnamon, cardamom, and *kaila* along with *kesara*, each measuring one *pala*.
When well-cooled, one should consume here a honey-measure of the size of a *bilva* fruit, or a *karṣa* measure, every morning.
(2) The aphrodisiac electuary beginning with *śṛṅgāṭaka*:
One *pala* of *śṛṅgāṭaka* and one *pala* of *vārāhikanda* should be prepared;
having been powdered, strained through cloth, and fried with clarified butter, it is then combined with sugar. (YRps 12.12)
One should take one *pala* each of cloves, black agallochum, and saffron, along with a tenth part of milk.
Having properly prepared this linctus, one should certainly consume it in the measure of one *karṣa* every morning.
It indeed quickly awakens desire; one shall delight in women and become like a sparrow. (YRps 12.13)

(3) The *avaleha* that kindles desire and acts as an aphrodisiac: Having powdered all of these—*śatāvarī*, *gokṣura*, the root of *darbha*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *nāgabalā*, and *ātmaguptā*—one *pala* each, they should be cooked with ten parts of milk. YRps 12.14.
Ten *pala* of sugar should be added here; one should prepare the cooking by means of the application of fire.
When consumed soaked in honey, it always produces an intense arousal of desire within half a watch (*yāma*).
It suddenly brings about an increase in vigor, an increase in the digestive fire, and an increase in the fire of passion.
(4) The *avaleha* (linctus) that acts as an aphrodisiac, made from black gram and other ingredients:
one *āḍhaka* each of fresh black gram (*māṣa*) and seeds of *ātmaguptā*,
along with *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *jīvā*, *medā*, *vṛddhi*, and *śatāvarī*.
One should prepare a decoction of madhuka and aśvagandhā, each measured at one prasṛta;
into that liquid, one should add one prastha of cow's ghee and ten times as much milk.
Having added one *prastha* of the fresh juice of *vidārī* and one *prastha* of sugarcane juice, it should be cooked over a gentle fire; once prepared, the clarified butter should be set aside.
One should add four palas each of sugar, tugākṣīrī, and honey, and one pala of long pepper (pippalī) to that.
Having first licked one *pala* of this from here, one should then consume food, if one desires imperishable semen and the supreme strength of the penis. (YRps 12.21)
YRps, Chapter 13 (Vīryastambhakarī Vaṭī): Śrīvāsa, mastakī, nāgakesara, and lavaṅgaka.
Kaṅkola, tulasī seeds, khurāsānī, and ahiphenaka.
And [one should take] *jāvitrikā*, dried ginger, saffron, *kaṅkolaka*, *tugākṣīrī*, and nutmeg, in equal parts. (YRps 13.2)
Having thus pulverized all these ingredients, one should place them inside a coconut shell and cook them in milk for five days.
One should take [the substance] from a coconut fruit and grind it with honey;
a pill the size of a jujube fruit (kola) should indeed be consumed at the beginning of the night.
It produces a fierce rigidity of effort, lasting for a period of four watches.
(The Pill that Causes the Retention of Semen): Clove, pure camphor, jasmine leaf, and likewise the fruit;
saffron, gold-seed (*Cannabis sativa*), and the flower of *Datura*. YRps 13.6.
One should grind together the root and bark of *abdhiśoṣa* and all [the other ingredients] in one place;
this cleansing preparation should be prepared by adding one part [of it] to cow’s milk.
One part of the powder derived from *bhṛṅgī* leaves and one part of golden ochre (*svarṇagairika*) should be infused twenty-one times with the juice of *postaka*.
The wise physician should prepare a pill that causes the stabilization of semen.
(The Pill that Stops the Flow of Semen):

Take nutmeg, arka-root, karahāṭa, cloves, dry ginger, kaṅkola, saffron, long pepper, and yellow sandalwood; combine these in equal parts with opium and white mica. Having prepared these, one should form pills with honey.

Measuring two māṣas each, those who desire love should consume this at night and immediately drink sweet buffalo milk thereafter, so that they may arrest their emissions and captivate the hearts of the skilled women.
(The medicinal pill that causes the stiffening of virility):
The virile substance produced from the shoulder region of the *dardura* [frog], combined with camphor and the powder of *karahāṭa*, [forms the pill]. (YRps 13.11)
Having crushed it, one should prepare a powder and make pills the size of a mung bean;
after rubbing them with saliva, one should apply them as an ointment to the penis.
One should hold the bindu for half a yāma, just as one accepts the word of the guru as truth.
(Śukrastambhakacūrṇam):
One *pala* of *postaka*, one *karṣa* of ginger, and one *pala* of sugar, along with one *karṣa* of cinnamon bark, when drunk with milk, certainly retains the semen. (YRps 13.14)

This work, which brings joy to the hearts of the learned, has been composed by his son, the poet Yaśodhara, a physician of noble character; may it constantly produce happiness in the minds of the virtuous. He is a wise man of the Śrī Goḍa lineage, an ocean of the sport of learning, whose mind is devoted to the worship of the glorious Gaṅgādhara. YRps 13.15.

Among all lands, the kingdom of the gods is the most excellent; therein lies a fortress named Jīrṇa, which is graced by Brahmins devoted to the Vedas and Śāstras. In that place, the illustrious Padmanābha—who takes delight in the lotus feet of Śambhu—himself composed this work, along with his son, the poet Yaśodhara.

For the enlightenment of the virtuous, for the happiness of those afflicted by disease, for the complete accomplishment of the aims of his disciples, for the livelihood of physicians, for the benefit of the learned, and indeed for the destruction of anxiety— the most skillful Śrī Bhaṭṭa Yaśodhara, son of Śrī Padmanābha and a preeminent poet, himself composed this work in the ancient city of Śrī Durga.
